Fact.Name: Earnings on excess contributions, or zero when unanswered
Fact.Description: The earnings on excess contributions, or zero if unanswered

Fact.Name: Earnings on excess contributions that belong on THIS return, or zero
Fact.Description:
The per-item addend of /hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome, scoped to the filer(s) of this return: the primary filer's item always, the secondary filer's item only on a joint return, $0 otherwise.
WHY THE SCOPING IS OWED HERE AND NOWHERE ELSE ON THIS MODULE'S PART II ROUTES. Form 8889 is a PER-INDIVIDUAL form — https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 4 (LEFT column), "If married filing jointly and both you and" / "your spouse have HSAs, complete a separate Form 8889 for" / "each of you." — and the two printed lines that add the two forms together, Schedule 1 line 8f and Schedule 2 line 17c, carry a spouse's figure only because IRC 6013(a) put the spouse on this return. Every OTHER aggregate this module routes to those lines is built out of /filers/*/… facts whose secondary arm is already All(filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ, ../isSecondaryFiler) over a Dollar 0 default: /filers/*/totalHsaDistributions (line 14a), /filers/*/hsaRolloverTotal and /filers/*/hsaTotalExcessContributionsWithdrawnInTime (line 14b) and /filers/*/hsaQualifiedMedExpenses (line 15). So on a non-joint return the secondary filer's line 14c is Incomplete, their line 16 falls to the un-gated Dollar 0 Case, and neither /hsaCollectionRouteTaxableDistributions nor /hsaCollectionRouteAdditionalTax20PctTotal carries their amount.
/hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome WAS THE ONE THAT WAS NOT SCOPED, and this fact is the whole of the fix. That fact is a CollectionSum straight over /hsaDistributions/*/earningsOnExcessContributionsOrZero, so it summed every item's Form 1099-SA box 2 regardless of whose form it was, and it is an addend of income /schedule1TotalOtherIncome. Measured on the same fixture: 550.00 before (the primary's 150.00 plus the spouse's 400.00), 150.00 after.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0 OFF-POPULATION, which is load-bearing because the consumer is an addend of a shipping income total. ../belongsToPrimaryFiler and ../belongsToSecondaryFiler both read filers:/primaryFiler, Incomplete on a graph with no filers, and filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ is Incomplete until /filingStatus is answered — so all three reads sit inside All(IsComplete(x), x), which makes an Incomplete operand's Case resolve FALSE rather than leaving the Switch Incomplete, and the True-arm $0 catches every such item.
THE FILTERED COLLECTIONS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT USED. /primaryFilerHsaDistributions and /secondaryFilerHsaDistributions are un-defaulted Switches on /primaryFiler/hasHsaCanHaveDistribution and /secondaryFiler/hasHsaCanHaveDistribution, so a CollectionSum over either resolves Incomplete for a filer who cannot have distributions and would degrade a total that is Complete on every committed case. The per-item attribution test carries no such gate.
THE GUARD IS UNTOUCHED AND THAT IS NOT A CONTRADICTION. /hsaDistributions/secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ still refuses the very return this fact now totals correctly: scoping stops the ARITHMETIC from overstating, but the spouse's Form 1099-SA still has no line of this return to sit on, which is an input contradiction rather than an unbuilt computation.

Fact.Name: HSA excess contribution earnings other income
Fact.Description:
Total earnings on excess contributions withdrawn before the due date, to be included in Schedule 1 other income, for the filer(s) of this return.
The addend is /hsaDistributions/*/earningsOnExcessContributionsThisReturnOrZero rather than /hsaDistributions/*/earningsOnExcessContributionsOrZero: Form 8889 is per individual and only IRC 6013(a) puts a second one on this 1040, so a non-joint return that carries the spouse's Form 1099-SA must not add its box 2 here. The reasoning and the authorities are on the addend.
Distribution code options for 1099-SA Box3

Who received a death-code (box 3 code 4 or 6) HSA distribution: the decedent's surviving spouse designated beneficiary, the decedent's estate, or this filer as a nonspouse designated beneficiary. The answer is what picks between IRC 223(f)(8)'s outcomes - the code alone cannot, because code 4 covers BOTH the estate (any year) and any beneficiary paid in the year of death: the surviving-spouse case is 223(f)(8)(A) (the HSA is treated as if the spouse were the account beneficiary, so the distribution runs the spouse's own ordinary chain); the estate and nonspouse cases are 223(f)(8)(B) (the account ceases to be an HSA and the date-of-death fair market value is includible - in the decedent's final-year gross income for the estate, in the acquirer's gross income otherwise).

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-SA reports a box 3 code 4 death distribution (other than code 6)
Fact.Description: Whether this Form 1099-SA's box 3 carries code 4, "Death distribution other than code 6": a payment to the decedent's estate (in or after the year of death), or a payment to a beneficiary in the year of death. One of the two per-item detectors the distribution-code switch mints so the IRC 223(f)(8) death treatment can tell the two death codes apart: WHICH code decides WHOSE gross income the 223(f)(8)(B) fair-market-value inclusion lands in (the estate case puts it on the decedent's final return, the nonspouse-beneficiary case on the beneficiary's). Complete-safe FALSE while box 3 is unanswered, so nothing downstream can go Incomplete by contagion. It is the second disjunct of conjunct (1) of ../isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution, so a code-4 item answered "filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary" on ../writableDeathDistributionRecipient, with box 4 and the pre-death qualified expenses answered, COMPUTES the IRC 223(f)(8)(B) inclusion. The recipient answer is the whole of the discrimination this detector cannot do on its own: code 4 also covers the decedent's ESTATE (in or after the year of death), which ../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution admits only on the decedent's own final return and which refuses otherwise (see /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout), and the SURVIVING SPOUSE paid in the year of death, which is ../isAdmittedSurvivingSpouseDeathDistribution.

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-SA reports a box 3 code 6 death distribution (nonspouse beneficiary, after the year of death)
Fact.Description: Whether this Form 1099-SA's box 3 carries code 6, "Death distribution after year of death to a nonspouse beneficiary": a payment to the decedent's nonspouse beneficiary, other than an estate, after the year of death. The second per-item detector the distribution-code switch mints for the IRC 223(f)(8) death treatment - see the code 4 sibling above for why the split matters. This is the code whose recipient CAN be a filer of this 1040 (the beneficiary reporting the 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(II) inclusion, reduced by the decedent's pre-death qualified expenses under 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I)); the spouse designated beneficiary never appears under either death code, because the 1099-SA instructions give that distribution code 1 and 223(f)(8)(A) treats the account as the spouse's own HSA. Complete-safe FALSE while box 3 is unanswered. A code-6 item whose recipient is answered "filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary" and which carries both box 4 and the pre-death qualified-expenses intake is ADMITTED through ../isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution and computes. Every other code-6 item refuses the return through /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout: the completeness residue (any of those three unanswered), the two document/answer contradictions (a spouse or estate recipient answer on a code-6 form), and the rollover/withdrawn-excess contradictions (a YES to either on the item).

Fact.Name: This death-code Form 1099-SA is the surviving spouse designated beneficiary's own distribution and is admitted
Fact.Description: Whether this Form 1099-SA is a box 3 code 4 death distribution whose recipient the filer answered as the decedent's SURVIVING SPOUSE designated beneficiary - the IRC 223(f)(8)(A) case. Under (A) the HSA is treated as if the spouse were the account beneficiary, and the Form 8889 instructions say the same in as many words ("The surviving spouse completes Form 8889 as though the HSA belonged to the surviving spouse"), so an admitted item runs the ordinary chain unchanged: line 16 inclusion for any part not covered by qualified medical expenses, the 20% additional tax with the attestation pair as its exception vehicle, and the unattested-taxable refusal exactly as for a code-1 item. An admitted item is excluded from BOTH residual death refusals: the code knockout (/filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout) and the box-4 FMV knockout (../causesFmvKnockout) - box 4 is informational here, because under (A) nothing is includible by reason of the death at all. The (B) fair-market-value inclusion arises only in the estate and nonspouse cases, which their own admissions compute (../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution, ../isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution). The admissions are DISJOINT on the recipient answer - this one requires survivingSpouseBeneficiary, the (B) ones decedentEstate or filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary, and ../writableDeathDistributionRecipient carries exactly one answer - so no item can be admitted by two of them. REQUIRES CODE 4: a code-6 item never admits, even with a surviving-spouse recipient answer, because the 1099-SA instructions give the spouse's after-year distribution code 1 - code 6 with a spouse answer is a document/answer contradiction, and the return stays refused on the code. Complete-safe FALSE while box 3 or the recipient is unanswered, so the death refusal stands until both are answered and nothing downstream goes Incomplete by contagion.

Fact.Name: This death-code Form 1099-SA is a filer's own IRC 223(f)(8)(B) inclusion and is admitted
Fact.Description:
The ADMISSION for a nonspouse designated beneficiary's death distribution. It narrows the death-code arms of /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout and the matching arm of ../causesFmvKnockout. The decedent's pre-death qualified expenses under IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) have their intake (../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses) and the three Part II quantities are computed by the siblings below, so an item that carries every input is admitted and runs the ordinary Part II chain with the box-4 value on line 14a.
THE SIX CONJUNCTS, each a separate completeness residue or contradiction if it fails: (1) box 3 is a DEATH code - code 6 (../isDeathDistributionToNonspouseAfterYearOfDeath) or code 4 (../isDeathDistributionOtherThanCode6); each is itself complete-safe FALSE while box 3 is unanswered, so the Any over them is too. The code is NOT the discriminator: IRC 223(f)(8)(B) and the i8889 "Death of Account Beneficiary" section key on the beneficiary not being the surviving spouse and say nothing about the box-3 code, and the 1099-SA instructions give the SAME beneficiary's payment code 4 when the trustee pays it in the year of death and code 6 when after (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2 and https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2). Conjunct (2) is the discriminator, and it is what keeps the code-4 ESTATE and the code-4 SURVIVING-SPOUSE cases out of this arm; (2) the recipient answer is "filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary" - the beneficiary is a FILER of this return. A code-6 item answered "surviving spouse" is a document/answer contradiction (the spouse's after-year distribution carries code 1, not 6) and one answered "estate" is another (code 6 is defined as "other than an estate"); both stay refused, and so does an unanswered recipient. On a CODE-4 item neither other answer is a contradiction and both are still NOT admitted here, for different reasons that are both correct: "surviving spouse" is the IRC 223(f)(8)(A) case and is admitted by ../isAdmittedSurvivingSpouseDeathDistribution instead, and "estate" puts the inclusion on the DECEDENT'S final income tax return (i8889, "If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3), which ../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution admits when the item's owning filer is the one marked deceased on this return. Where this return is NOT the decedent's final return the estate refusal is correct and permanent; (3) box 4 is answered (../writableFmvOnDateOfDeath). Box 4 IS the inclusion - "an amount equal to the fair market value of the assets in such account on such date" - so an unanswered box 4 leaves nothing to include. Without this conjunct the admission would release both guards and then take the whole Part II chain Incomplete on an unanswered Writable, which is a return that neither files nor refuses; (4) the pre-death expenses are answered. An unknown reduction cannot be defaulted to 0 without silently taxing the whole account; (5) the box-1 rollover boolean ../writableDistributionsRolloverBool is answered AND false; (6) the excess-contribution boolean ../hasWithdrawnExcessContributions is answered AND false. WHY (5) AND (6), the third document/answer contradiction this admission refuses: printed line 14b is defined as a subtraction FROM line 14a ("Distributions included on line 14a that you rolled over to another HSA"), and on an admitted item line 14a is the date-of-death fair market value rather than box 1. IRC 223(f)(5) admits a rollover only as a payment into a health savings account "of such beneficiary", and 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(I) killed the account on the date of death, so a nonspouse beneficiary can neither roll the inherited value over nor have had a timely-returned excess contribution in it. Without these conjuncts one answered boolean would erase the WHOLE inclusion on a return that FILES: measured without them, on the release witness plus a true rollover boolean and an $8,000 rollover amount, line 14a 9,000, line 14b 8,000, line 14c 1,000, line 15 2,000, line 16 0.00 and Schedule 1 line 8f 0.00, with /flowIsKnockedOut Placeholder false. The rollover question is asked on EVERY Form 1099-SA (/hsaDistributions/*/isComplete requires it), so this is not exotic.
THE IsComplete FENCES ARE LOAD-BEARING AND MUST NOT BE DROPPED. Both booleans are bare Writable Booleans and ../isComplete is a separate fact that does not gate this one, so a naked Not over an unanswered Boolean would take the inner All Incomplete, this admission Incomplete, the Switch in ../form8889Line14aItemAmount Incomplete and /filers/*/totalHsaDistributions Incomplete mid-interview on a code-6 item - the "neither files nor refuses" posture conjunct (3) exists to prevent. Measured with the fences in place, on the release witness with the rollover boolean simply UNANSWERED: this admission Complete false, ../form8889Line14aItemAmount Complete 8,000.00 (the box-1 True arm) and /filers/*/totalHsaDistributions Complete 8,000.00 - Complete, not Incomplete.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE by the module's All(IsComplete(x), x) idiom, so the death refusal stands until every input is answered and nothing downstream goes Incomplete by contagion.
THE CODE-4 NONSPOUSE CASE IS THE STATUTORILY CLEAN ONE: IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(II) puts the inclusion in "the taxable year which includes" the date of death, and a code-4 form is by its own definition issued FOR that year (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2), so the year-of-death timing question the code-6 arm carries - an open owner question - does not arise on this arm at all.
WHAT THIS ADMISSION DOES NOT COVER: the code-4 ESTATE case, which ../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution admits on the decedent's own final return; and then four correct PERMANENT refusals: any of the six conjuncts unanswered (data completeness); the two recipient contradictions on a code-6 form; the two rollover/excess contradictions on either code; and code 5 with no January-1 value, which is a different arm entirely. The four measured GAPS the treatment carries - no per-decedent aggregate cap, the one-directional clamp, post-death earnings, and the IRC 691(c) estate-tax deduction - are recorded in full on records /hsaDeathOfAccountBeneficiaryTreatment; they are properties of the (beneficiary, decedent) arithmetic and not of the code.

Fact.Name: This code-4 Form 1099-SA is the decedent's own estate inclusion on the decedent's final return, and is admitted
Fact.Description:
The ADMISSION that narrows the code-4 estate residue of ../causesFmvKnockout and /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout. IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i) puts the date-of-death fair market value in "the gross income of such beneficiary for the taxable year which includes such date", and where the beneficiary is the account holder's own estate the beneficiary is the account holder, so the inclusion is on the DECEDENT'S OWN final income tax return - i8889 says so directly ("If the account beneficiary's estate is the beneficiary, the value of the HSA as of the date of death is included on the account beneficiary's final income tax return", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3). This dictionary can carry that return: a deceased primary filer's surviving spouse or executor files Form 1040 on the decedent's behalf (form1040 /writableForm1040PrimaryFilerDeceased) and a deceased secondary filer's surviving spouse files the IRC 6013(a)(3) joint final return (filers /inScopeDeceasedSpouse) - both ship, and this fact is the one in this module that reads them.
THE FIVE CONJUNCTS, each a separate completeness or contradiction residue if it fails: (1) box 3 is code 4 (../isDeathDistributionOtherThanCode6). Code 6 is defined as a nonspouse beneficiary "other than an estate" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 3), so an estate distribution can only ever carry code 4 - a code-6 item answered "estate" is the document/answer contradiction ../isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution's own Description names and stays refused; (2) the recipient answer is "decedentEstate" (../writableDeathDistributionRecipient). The recipient answer is the whole discrimination between this arm and the code-4 surviving-spouse and nonspouse-beneficiary arms, exactly as it is for those two; (3) box 4 is answered (../writableFmvOnDateOfDeath) - the inclusion itself, so an unanswered box 4 leaves nothing to include; (4) the item's OWNING FILER is the one marked deceased on THIS return - own-filer, complete-safe: ../belongsToPrimaryFiler AND an answered, true form1040:/writableForm1040PrimaryFilerDeceased, OR ../belongsToSecondaryFiler AND an answered, true filers:/inScopeDeceasedSpouse. An estate item belonging to the OTHER filer, or to either filer on a return where neither is marked deceased, is a REAL residue: the estate's own Form 1099-SA carries the estate's TIN and reports to the estate's own return, which this dictionary does not file, so the refusal there is correct and permanent rather than a completeness gap this screen closes; (5) the rollover and withdrawn-excess-contributions booleans are both answered AND false, the same document/answer contradiction ../isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution refuses on: IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(I) ends the account on the date of death for EITHER (B) case, estate or nonspouse beneficiary alike, so an estate item can be rolled into no HSA and can hold no timely-returned excess contribution either.
NO PRE-DEATH-EXPENSES CONJUNCT, DELIBERATELY, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE THIS ADMISSION DIVERGES FROM THE NONSPOUSE ONE. 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduces the inclusion "of any person OTHER THAN THE ESTATE" by the decedent's pre-death qualified medical expenses (26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024, the parenthetical at line 421), and i8889 says the same to the filer: "On Part II, line 15, for a beneficiary OTHER THAN THE ESTATE, enter qualified medical expenses" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3, emphasis this dictionary's). The estate gets no reduction at all, so this admission does not read ../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses and ../form8889Line15ItemAmount routes an admitted estate item straight to $0 rather than to a clamp.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE by the module's All(IsComplete(x), x) idiom on every writable-backed conjunct, so the estate refusal stands until every input is answered and nothing downstream goes Incomplete by contagion.

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-SA's contribution to printed Form 8889 line 14a
Fact.Description:
What this item puts on its owner's Form 8889 line 14a: the box-4 fair market value on the date of death for an ADMITTED nonspouse-beneficiary or estate death distribution, and box 1 (../writableGrossDistribution) for every other item.
THE SELECT IS THE INSTRUCTION, not a preference. i8889's beneficiary bullet says "On Part II, line 14a, enter the fair market value of the HSA as of the date of death" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3) and says nothing about box 1, because on this item box 1 is not a distribution from a health savings account at all: IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(I) has the account CEASE to be an HSA as of the date of death (26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024), so what the trustee later paid the beneficiary is a payment of inherited property whose value is already inside box 4. Adding the two would include the same dollars twice, and the direction would be taxpayer-ADVERSE. This is the same shape of question the section 4975 deemed distribution answered the other way on /filers/*/totalHsaDistributions, and it is answered differently here for a reason the sources state: there the instructions add a value the 1099-SA does not report, here they REPLACE the value it does.
BOX 1 UNCHANGED ON EVERY ITEM THAT IS NOT AN ADMITTED DEATH ITEM, structurally: the True arm is the bare Writable, so an item with box 1 unanswered stays Incomplete exactly as a direct read of box 1 would, and the collection sums above it keep their posture.

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-SA's contribution to printed Form 8889 line 15
Fact.Description:
What this item puts on its owner's Form 8889 line 15: for an ADMITTED nonspouse-beneficiary death distribution, the decedent's pre-death qualified medical expenses the beneficiary paid within a year of the death, CLAMPED at the item's own box 4; for an ADMITTED estate death distribution, $0 (223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) excludes the estate from the reduction entirely - see the Derived Case below for the full argument); for every other item, the ordinary line-15 answer ../writableQualifiedMedExpenses unchanged.
THE CLAMP IS THE STATUTE'S, not the form's, and it is the one place where the two disagree. IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduces "the amount includible in gross income under clause (i)", so the reduction is bounded by that inclusion and cannot drive it below zero; the printed line 15 carries no such cap, and on a filer who ALSO holds an ordinary Form 1099-SA an uncapped aggregate would let the decedent's expenses erase the taxable part of a distribution that has nothing to do with the death. Clamping per item keeps the reduction where the statute puts it. The direction of the choice is taxpayer-ADVERSE relative to a literal aggregate reading, which is the direction this dictionary takes when the two readings differ.
THE FORM-SIDE READING THAT SUPPORTS THE CLAMP, and it is a READING and not an authority. i8889's Note has a beneficiary of two or more HSAs, or of an inherited HSA plus their own, file a STATEMENT Form 8889 per account and a CONTROLLING Form 8889 ("combining the amounts shown on each of the statement Forms 8889"), https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3. Each statement form runs its own line 16, which floors at zero, and that is exactly what the per-item clamp reproduces. THE HONEST STATEMENT OF ITS STRENGTH: "combining the amounts shown" can equally be read as combining 14a, 14b and 15 line by line and letting the controlling form's own line 16 recompute, which is the reading /filers/*/hsaQualifiedMedExpenses actually implements. The clamp wins on the taxpayer-adverse tie-break, not on the text, and this cite does NOT take this fact off interpretation:provisional.
TWO NAMED GAPS THIS FACT KEEPS, both consequences of that same reading and neither built here. (1) NO PER-DECEDENT AGGREGATE CAP: the statute reduces the inclusion of a person by a DECEDENT's expenses, so the correct granularity is the (beneficiary, decedent) pair, which the per-item clamp equals only where one account was inherited from that decedent. The dictionary holds no decedent identity; the split is instructed on the screen (../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses) and not enforced. Measured: the same $8,000 of one decedent's expenses entered on two inherited $9,000 accounts gives $16,000 of reduction, line 16 $2,000 against the statute's $10,000, taxpayer-FAVOURABLE. (2) THE CLAMP RUNS IN ONE DIRECTION ONLY: it stops the decedent's expenses spilling ONTO an unrelated Form 1099-SA, but nothing stops an ordinary item that OVER-SPENDS from spilling onto the death inclusion, because /filers/*/hsaQualifiedMedExpenses aggregates. Measured: a code-6 item with a $9,000 inclusion beside an ordinary item of box 1 $1,000 against $5,000 of qualified expenses puts $5,000 on Schedule 1 line 8f where the statement/controlling reading gives $9,000 - $4,000 short, again taxpayer-FAVOURABLE, and 20%-exempt either way so only the income line moves. Building a per-item floor on the ORDINARY side would change the aggregation behaviour for two ordinary HSAs, where it is defensible, so it is deliberately NOT built and is recorded as the residue of records /hsaNonNormalDistributionCodeTreatment.

Fact.Name: The IRC 223(f)(8)(B) inclusion this item carries, the part of line 16 that bears no 20% tax
Fact.Description:
Box 4 minus the clamped pre-death expenses, for an ADMITTED nonspouse-beneficiary death distribution; the RAW box 4 value, with no subtrahend, for an ADMITTED estate death distribution (../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution - IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduces the inclusion only of a person other than the estate); $0 on every other item. This is the portion of the owner's printed Form 8889 line 16 that arises from the death rather than from an unqualified distribution, and it is carried up to /filers/*/hsaAdditionalTaxExceptionAmountDerived so that the 20% additional tax does not reach it.
THE 20% TAX DOES NOT APPLY, and the instruction is flat rather than hedged: i8889's "Death of Account Beneficiary" section ends "The distribution is not subject to the additional 20% tax" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3) - contrast the deemed-distribution section three paragraphs earlier, which says "Generally, these distributions are subject to the additional 20% tax". The statute agrees by its own terms: IRC 223(f)(4)(A) increases "the tax imposed by this chapter on the ACCOUNT BENEFICIARY" by 20 percent of an amount "includible in gross income under paragraph (2)", and this inclusion is neither - it is includible under (f)(8)(B)(i) and the person including it is the beneficiary's successor, not the account beneficiary. There is therefore no open question here of the kind /flowKnockoutHsaDistributionFMV's pledge arm carries.
IT IS AN EXCEPTION TO THE ADDITIONAL TAX, NOT TO THE INCOME INCLUSION - the distinction /filers/*/hsaAdditionalTaxExceptionAmountDerived's own Description draws. Line 16 and Schedule 1 line 8f carry the full amount; only the printed lines 17a/17b and Schedule 2 line 17c change.
NON-NEGATIVE by construction (the subtrahend is clamped at the minuend), and $0 rather than Incomplete on every non-admitted item, so the collection sums above it are complete-safe.

Fact.Name: This Form 1099-SA reports a box 3 code 5 prohibited-transaction distribution
Fact.Description:
Whether this Form 1099-SA's box 3 carries code 5, "Prohibited transaction". The 1099-SA table's own explanation of the code is a bare pointer, "See sections 220(e)(2) and 223(e)(2)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 3), and 223(e)(2) applies "rules similar to" IRC 408(e)(2) and (4): under 408(e)(2)(A) the account ceases to be an HSA as of the FIRST DAY of the taxable year, and under 408(e)(2)(B) paragraph (d)(1) applies "as if there were a distribution on such first day in an amount equal to the fair market value (on such first day) of all assets in the account".
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE. The box 3 answer is an optional Writable with no default, so the IsComplete conjunct is what keeps this detector (and everything reading it) resolvable mid-interview.

Fact.Name: A code 5 item whose owner has supplied the January 1 fair market value
Fact.Description:
The ADMISSION that narrows the code-5 arm of /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout. The deemed distribution a prohibited transaction causes is the account's January-1 fair market value, which is NOT box 1 of the Form 1099-SA; its intake is ../filer/writableHsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv, so an item whose OWNING FILER has answered it is admitted and runs the ordinary Part II chain with the January-1 value on line 14a. An item whose owner has NOT answered refuses - that is the data-completeness residue the guard keeps, and it is the correct permanent refusal, because without the January-1 value the return would tax box 1 (a number the statute does not use) instead of the whole account.
THE OWNER, NOT THE RETURN. The test is ../filer/hsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1FmvIsUsable (the owner answered AND the owner's Form 8889 Part II exists - that fact records why the second conjunct is load-bearing) rather than a return-level "somebody answered", because Form 8889 is a per-individual form (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 4, "If married filing jointly and both you and your spouse have HSAs, complete a separate Form 8889 for each of you") and line 14a is a per-filer fact. On an MFJ return where only one spouse had the prohibited transaction, the other spouse's Form 8889 must not carry the amount and their code-5 item, if any, must not be admitted by their spouse's answer.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE, by the module's own All(IsComplete(x), x) idiom over the filer dereference: ../filer is Incomplete on an item whose filer link is not yet answered, so the read is fenced.

Fact.Name: Some Form 1099-SA on this return carries box 3 code 5
Fact.Description: Return-level projection of /hsaDistributions/*/isProhibitedTransactionDistribution. Half of /hsaDeemedDistributionSection4975Triggered below; complete-safe false because its per-item operand is.

Fact.Name: This return reports a section 4975 prohibited transaction, on either intake route
Fact.Description:
The ASKED-WHEN gate of /filers/*/writableHsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv, and the gate its complete-safe alias reads. TRUE when either intake route says a section 4975 prohibited transaction happened: a Form 1099-SA in the collection carrying box 3 code 5, or the return-level attestation form8889 /hasNonNormalTopLevelHsaDistribution (the filer who has no Form 1099-SA at all, which is the ordinary case - the module header of dictionary/ty2025/form8889.xml records why that attestation is return-level and not per-document).
WHY THE AMOUNT FACT GATES ON THIS AND NOT ON THE ANSWER ALONE. A January-1 fair market value is only a deemed distribution if a prohibited transaction occurred; an answer left behind by an edited interview would otherwise inflate Form 8889 line 14a with no refusal anywhere to catch it, which is taxpayer-ADVERSE. Gating the amount on the trigger makes the screen's own asked-when enforceable in the graph. The residue this creates is named on /filers/*/hsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv.
Complete-safe false: both operands are.

Fact.Name: hsa distribution code 1099-SA
Fact.Description:
Box 3 of Form 1099-SA: Distribution code. This is the six-valued code the whole non-normal-distribution machinery switches on: /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout admits codes 1, 2 and 3, the admitted code-4 cases (surviving spouse, nonspouse beneficiary, and the estate on the decedent's own final return), the admitted code-5 case and the admitted code-6 nonspouse-beneficiary case, and refuses the rest.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION (the application builds this screen from this Description without opening an IRS document). The specification is supplied here rather than on a new writable because the intake already exists and "one quantity, one fact" forbids minting a second one.
THE QUESTION: "What distribution code is in box 3 of this Form 1099-SA?"
HELP TEXT: "Box 3 of Form 1099-SA carries a one-digit code that tells us what kind of distribution this was. Copy the code exactly as the trustee printed it - it changes how the money is taxed." (Paraphrasing 2025 Instructions for Forms 1099-SA and 5498-SA, "Box 3. Distribution Code": "Enter the appropriate distribution code from the following list that shows the type of distribution"; https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, pages 2-3, a two-column extraction whose LEFT column carries the code labels and whose RIGHT column carries their explanations.)
ASKED WHEN: on every /hsaDistributions item - one answer per Form 1099-SA, on the same screen as box 1 (../writableGrossDistribution) and box 2 (../writableEarningsOnExcessContributions). There is no gating fact: a filer who is entering a Form 1099-SA at all has a box 3 in front of them.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: REFUSED. /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout's residue (e) refuses an item whose code is unanswered, the same data-completeness ground as the death-recipient/box-4/pre-death-expenses residue (b) - an unanswered code does not run the item through the ordinary chain as though it were a normal distribution. The application should still treat this field as REQUIRED on the screen (row 136) so the filer is asked rather than refused; the dictionary refusal is the backstop for an answer the screen fails to collect.
VALIDATION: Enum over /hsaDistributionCodeOptions. Six options, and these are the PRINTED labels from the instructions' own table ("Distribution Codes for Distributions From HSAs, Archer MSAs, and Medicare Advantage MSAs", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 3), which the application should render verbatim beside the digit: normalDistribution -> "1—Normal distributions" excessContributions -> "2—Excess contributions" disability -> "3—Disability" deathOtherThanCode6 -> "4—Death distribution other than code 6" prohibitedTransaction -> "5—Prohibited transaction" deathDistributionAfterYear -> "6—Death distribution after year of death to a nonspouse beneficiary" The dash is the EM DASH the source prints, character for character (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 3 render "1—Normal distributions"). This is element text, so an em dash is legal; only XML COMMENTS forbid the double hyphen. No Min/Max; exactly one option; no free text.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS, option by option, so the screen can be honest about consequences: 1 - runs the ordinary Part II chain (lines 14a/14c/15/16) and the 20% additional tax with the attestation pair as its only exception vehicle; 2 - routes to the return-of-excess machinery (/hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome and /hsaExcessContributionExciseTaxForm5329PartVii) as well as the ordinary chain; 3 - runs the ordinary chain; the IRC 223(f)(4)(B) forgiveness of the 20% tax is claimed on /filers/*/writableHsaCollectionExceptionReason (option "disability"), NOT derived from this code; 4 - opens the recipient question ../writableDeathDistributionRecipient, and answered "this filer as nonspouse beneficiary" it ALSO opens the pre-death qualified-expenses question ../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses, exactly as code 6 does. Answered "surviving spouse" the item is admitted as the IRC 223(f)(8)(A) case and runs the ordinary chain; answered "this filer as nonspouse beneficiary" with box 4 and the pre-death expenses present, the item is admitted as the IRC 223(f)(8)(B) year-of-death case and computes box 4 on Form 8889 line 14a, the pre-death expenses (clamped at box 4) on line 15, line 16 to Schedule 1 line 8f and NO 20% additional tax; answered "estate" the item is admitted only when its owning filer is the one marked deceased on this return (../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution: box 4 on the decedent's own line 14a, $0 on line 15, NO 20% additional tax) and the return is refused otherwise, because the inclusion belongs on the DECEDENT'S final return; left unanswered, or missing box 4 or the pre-death expenses on the nonspouse answer, the return is refused; AND THE SCREEN TEXT ON ROW 151 IS CODE-CONDITIONAL when it is opened from HERE: the help text's box-4 netting sentence and the year-of-death double-inclusion disclosure are BOTH code-6 only, and one of them is taxpayer-adverse if shipped on a code 4. The application branches on ../isDeathDistributionOtherThanCode6 versus ../isDeathDistributionToNonspouseAfterYearOfDeath (both exported); the two replacement sentences are marked at their point of use inside ../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses's Description. 5 - opens the January-1 fair-market-value question /filers/*/writableHsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv. Answered, the account's January-1 value lands on Form 8889 line 14a and the return computes; unanswered, the return is refused; 6 - opens the SAME recipient question as code 4 (../writableDeathDistributionRecipient) and, answered "this filer as nonspouse beneficiary", the SAME pre-death qualified-expenses question as code 4, ../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses. With that answer and box 4 present the item is admitted and computes: box 4 on Form 8889 line 14a, the pre-death expenses (clamped at box 4) on line 15, line 16 to Schedule 1 line 8f, and NO 20% additional tax. Unanswered on any of the three, or answered "surviving spouse" or "estate" (both contradictions on a code-6 form), the return is refused. The separately marked beneficiary Form 8889 that the i8889 "Death of Account Beneficiary" section prescribes is a PRINT obligation, recorded on the pre-death-expenses writable, and it moves no dollar.

Whether the filer is knocked out due to their HDHP coverage status. A part-year filer whose proration is computable AND has no employer-contribution excess (../hsaPartYearFreed) is not knocked out — the return computes the prorated Line 3 limit instead. All other part-year filers (no month input, mixed coverage, or employer contributions above the prorated limit) stay knocked out. All-year and no-HSA filers are unaffected (status is not partOfYear).

Fact.Name: Months of HDHP coverage (Form 8889 Line 3 Limitation Chart)
Fact.Description: the number of months (0-12) the filer had qualifying HDHP coverage, for the Form 8889 Line 3 Limitation-Chart proration of the annual limit when coverage is PART-YEAR. Optional/complete-safe: unanswered means no proration is computable, so the part-year knockout still refuses (World-#1-safe). Only the standard single-coverage-type proration is modeled.

Fact.Name: HDHP-eligible on December 1 (last-month rule, section 223(b)(8))
Fact.Description: whether the filer was an eligible individual (HDHP coverage) on December 1. Under the section 223(b)(8) last-month rule this allows the FULL annual limit for the year (not prorated), subject to a testing period the filer attests to — the multi-year testing- period recapture is not modelled. Optional/complete-safe (unanswered → standard proration).

Fact.Name: Annual HSA limit for the filer's coverage type (before proration)
Fact.Description: the full-year self-only or family HSA contribution limit for the filer's coverage type (family if covered by a family HDHP, else self-only), the base the Line 3 proration scales. Uses the same constants as the all-year hsaBaseContributionLimit.

Fact.Name: Either spouse had family HDHP coverage at any time in the year (IRC 223(b)(5))
Fact.Description:
Whether the filer or their spouse was covered by a FAMILY high deductible health plan at any time during the tax year. The trigger IRC 223(b)(5) and Form 8889 Lines 3, 6 and 7 are all keyed on, asked once for the return because the statute's condition is about the couple and not about either spouse alone.
WHY A NEW INTAKE RATHER THAN A DERIVATION. The obvious derivation - read both filers' ../typeOfHdhp - cannot establish the NEGATIVE on the common shape: on a couple where only one spouse participates in an HSA, the other spouse is never asked their coverage type, so their writable is unanswered forever and an IsComplete-guarded derivation could never conclude "no family coverage". It would free nobody. /hsaEitherSpouseHadFamilyCoverage therefore reads this attestation AND both raw writables, with the writables WINNING on contradiction.
COMPLETE-SAFE AND REFUSAL-SAFE, which are different properties and this fact needs both. Unanswered, /hsaEitherSpouseHadFamilyCoverage still resolves (so nothing goes Incomplete), and ../hsaPartYearMarriedSelfOnlyInScope still requires this writable to be Complete, so an unanswered married part-year return stays REFUSED.

Fact.Name: The IRC 223(b)(5) trigger, as this dictionary can establish it
Fact.Description:
True when family HDHP coverage is shown anywhere on the return: the attestation /writableHsaEitherSpouseHadFamilyCoverage answered YES, or either filer's own raw ../typeOfHdhp says "family" or "both". False otherwise, INCLUDING when nothing has been answered - which is safe here only because every consumer that could free a return pairs this with an explicit IsComplete on the attestation. Read that pairing as part of the fact.
THE RAW WRITABLES WIN OVER THE ATTESTATION, deliberately. A filer who answers "no family coverage" and separately enters family coverage as their own HDHP type has contradicted themselves; the Any resolves to TRUE, the return goes back to being refused, and no limit is computed off the more favourable of two answers.
The raw ../typeOfHdhp is used rather than ../typeOfHdhpDerived: the derived coverage facts cascade to Placeholder while the part-year knockout is still firing, which is circular, since these facts are what un-fire it. NOT A REPLACEMENT FOR /hsaMarriedFilersHaveFamilyCoverage, which is the all-year path's version of the same test and is left untouched. That one reads the DERIVED types and falls to False when either is Incomplete - correct where it is used, and useless here for exactly the reason above.

Fact.Name: The return has AFFIRMATIVELY established that neither spouse had family coverage
Fact.Description:
True only when the family-coverage question has actually been answered AND the answer (with both filers' own raw coverage types, which override it) comes out negative.
THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS AND Not(/hsaEitherSpouseHadFamilyCoverage) IS THE WHOLE POINT, and writing the second where the first is meant is the defect this fact exists to prevent. /hsaEitherSpouseHadFamilyCoverage falls to FALSE when nothing has been answered, because it is an Any over guarded conjuncts; negating it would therefore read "unanswered" as "no family coverage" and hand every married filer with an untouched interview a treatment reserved for couples who told us something. Requiring Complete makes "we do not know" behave as not established: the part-year return stays REFUSED, and the age-55 catch-up stays stripped on the married path. Every consumer of the 223(b)(5) condition on this path reads THIS fact, not the raw trigger.

Fact.Name: A married part-year filer the IRC 223(b)(5) sharing rule does not reach
Fact.Description:
True when this filer is MARRIED, has SELF-ONLY HDHP coverage of their own, and the return establishes that NEITHER spouse had family coverage at any time. That is precisely the married case IRC 223(b)(5) does not govern - its own opening clause is "if either spouse has family coverage" - so there is no shared family limit to divide and this filer's Form 8889 Line 3 is an ordinary per-filer Limitation-Chart proration.
THREE CONJUNCTS, EACH LOAD-BEARING, and the reason a weaker version would be wrong. (a) MARRIED: an unmarried filer takes the other branch of hsaPartYearProrationInScope and does not come through here at all. (b) SELF-ONLY specifically, not merely "not both": if THIS filer's own coverage is family then 223(b)(5)(A) deems both spouses family-covered and the whole sharing apparatus applies. Conjunct (c) would catch that through the raw writable, and this conjunct states it on the filer's own record besides. (c) THE ATTESTATION IS COMPLETE AND THE TRIGGER IS FALSE. Complete is required, not merely false-by-default: an unanswered return has not established anything, and freeing it would free every married part-year filer including the family-covered ones. Unanswered stays REFUSED.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT FREE, and each is refused by other machinery: a married filer with FAMILY or BOTH coverage (223(b)(5) sharing, unbuilt); an MFS return whose spouse also contributed (/flowKnockoutMFSLine6Check); a filer with no month-count input, mid-year-changing coverage, Medicare, or employer contributions above the prorated limit (hsaPartYearProrationInScope's other conjuncts and hsaPartYearFreed).

Fact.Name: Annual HSA limit the part-year proration scales (coverage-type limit + 55+ catch-up)
Fact.Description:
The per-month Form 8889 Line 3 Limitation-Chart amount × 12 = the coverage-type annual limit PLUS the §223(b)(3) $1,000 catch-up when the filer is 55+ and the Line 3 Note does not divert the catch-up to Line 7. This is the amount both the Limitation-Chart proration (× months / 12) and the last-month-rule full limit scale, so a part-year 55+ filer gets the prorated catch-up the chart includes for each eligible month (self-only 55+ = 5,300/mo; unmarried family 55+ = 9,550/mo). Used only inside hsaProratedContributionLimit.
THE CATCH-UP GATE IS NOT Not(/isMarried), and a bare marital test would be a latent trap: the diversion the Note describes is conditioned on "married AND had family coverage at any time", not on married alone, and the chart's SELF-ONLY branch carries no marital qualifier at all ("If you were age 55 or older at the end of 2025, enter $5,300 for the month" - only the FAMILY branch says "if, at the end of 2025, you were unmarried and age 55 or older"). A married 55+ filer with self-only coverage and no family coverage anywhere on the return therefore keeps the $5,300 chart amount, and the statute agrees: §223(b)(3)(A) increases the limitation for anyone who attained 55, with no marital condition anywhere in it.
ONE TENSION IN THE INSTRUCTIONS, NAMED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED OVER. The Line 3 narrative's item (6) grants the $1,000 to a filer who is "age 55 or older and unmarried or married with self-only HDHP coverage FOR THE ENTIRE YEAR" - and a part-year filer has self-only coverage for PART of the year. Read literally and in isolation that clause would deny the catch-up here. This dictionary follows the other reading, on grounds that are printed rather than inferred: item (6) increases "the amount determined in (3) or (4)", which are the NON-chart full-year shortcuts, and it closes by routing the chart case elsewhere in the same breath - "For the Line 3 Limitation Chart and Worksheet, the additional contribution amount is included for EACH MONTH you are an eligible individual." The chart then states the self-only amount with no marital and no full-year qualifier, and section 223(b)(3)(A), which the instructions implement rather than override, conditions the increase on attaining age 55 and on nothing else. So "for the entire year" qualifies item (6)'s own full-year branches, not the chart. THE OPPOSITE READING IS TAXPAYER-ADVERSE (a smaller Line 3), which is not a direction a doubt should be resolved in silently - hence the note.

Fact.Name: Prorated part-year HSA limit (Form 8889 Line 3)
Fact.Description: Form 8889 Line 3 for a PART-YEAR filer = the greater of (a) the last-month-rule FULL annual limit (if eligible on December 1, section 223(b)(8)) and (b) the Limitation-Chart proration = the with-catch-up annual limit (hsaProrationAnnualLimit — coverage-type limit plus the $1,000 catch-up when the filer is 55+ and the Line 3 Note does not divert it to Line 7) x months of coverage / 12, rounded. Used only inside hsaBaseContributionLimit's part-year case. A MARRIED self-only 55+ filer on a return with no family coverage anywhere keeps the catch-up on Line 3, which is what hsaProrationAnnualLimit computes.

Fact.Name: Part-year HSA proration is in scope (single coverage type + month input; U-069b: 55+ included; lane high-b: married self-only with no family coverage included)
Fact.Description: True when the filer has PART-YEAR HDHP coverage AND a single coverage type (not both self+family) AND a month-count input, and is either UNMARRIED or married with SELF-ONLY coverage on a return that establishes neither spouse had family coverage at any time (../hsaPartYearMarriedSelfOnlyInScope) — so the Line 3 proration is a purely per-filer computation. The with-catch-up annual limit (hsaProrationAnnualLimit) scales the $1,000 §223(b)(3) catch-up per the Line 3 chart, so 55+ filers get the correct prorated limit (self-only 55+ 6 mo = $2,650, not $2,150). Gates the hsaBaseContributionLimit part-year branch. Does NOT itself free the knockout — the excess-employer test does (see hsaPartYearFreed). WHY SOME MARRIED FILERS ARE IN SCOPE AND OTHERS ARE NOT. Under section 223(b)(5) / Form 8889 Line 6 a married couple with family coverage must SHARE one (prorated) family limit split between spouses (a cross-filer computation), and the all-year sharing logic (hasMetFamilyContributionLimitRule) is disabled for part-year — so a per-filer proration would give each spouse an independent limit and over-state the combined ceiling. That is true OF A COUPLE WITH FAMILY COVERAGE, and section 223(b)(5) reaches no other couple: its opening clause is "In the case of individuals who are married to each other, IF EITHER SPOUSE HAS FAMILY COVERAGE", and Form 8889's own Line 6 instruction opens the same way ("Spouses who have separate HSAs and had family coverage under an HDHP at any time during 2025"). A blanket Not(/isMarried) would refuse TWO populations under a reason that covers only one of them. ../hsaPartYearMarriedSelfOnlyInScope is the printed test, and it admits the other: a married part-year filer with SELF-ONLY coverage whose return establishes that neither spouse had family coverage at any time. Nothing is shared, so nothing is over-stated — and hasMetFamilyContributionLimitRule confirms it from the other side, since its own first conjunct is /hsaMarriedFilersHaveFamilyCoverage, which is false for exactly this couple. OUT OF SCOPE: married with family or "both" coverage (the sharing computation is unbuilt), and married with the family-coverage question UNANSWERED — Complete is required there, not merely false-by-default.

Fact.Name: Part-year filer freed from the coverage knockout (computable + no employer excess)
Fact.Description: True when the part-year proration is in scope AND the filer's employer contributions do NOT exceed the prorated Line 3 limit. When employer contributions EXCEED the prorated limit, the excess is taxable other income, and that case is not freed by this fact: it stays REFUSED by ../hsaHdhpCoverageStatusKnockout rather than silently understating income. All-year and no-HSA filers are false here.
Whether the filer has HSA distributions.

Whether the filer had coverage disqualifying HSA contributions.
WHY THE DERIVED READER AND NOT THE RAW WRITABLE. ../hadOtherCoverageIneligibleForHsaDerived is the flow-gated reader already used by /filers/*/causesOtherCoveragePartOfYearKnockOut and /filers/*/causesOtherCoverageWholeYearKnockOut, so this fact agrees with the two knockouts that stand on the same answer rather than diverging from them when the interview did not reach the question.
WHAT THE FALSE IT REPLACES ASSERTED. A hard False said, of every filer on every return, that no disqualifying coverage existed — the taxpayer-FAVOURABLE direction, which is why no filer complaint would ever surface it. This body keeps that answer wherever the question is unanswered and reverses it exactly where the filer said "wholeYear" or "partOfYear".
IsComplete IS NOT ON A COMPLETE-SAFE FACT HERE, which is the trap the brief names. ../hadOtherCoverageIneligibleForHsaDerived is a Switch with ONE Case and NO default, so it is genuinely Incomplete whenever ../flowShouldAskHadCoverageIneligibleForHSAContributions is false. The IsComplete is the real "source answered" predicate, not a tautology, and it is what makes this fact complete-safe FALSE on every return the interview never asked.
EITHER DURATION DISQUALIFIES, and the consumer is why. The only reader is ../wasEligibleToMakeHsaContributionsAllYear, which asks whether the filer was an eligible individual for EVERY month; IRC 223(c)(1)(A)(ii) denies eligibility for any month in which the individual is covered under a non-permitted plan, so one month of such coverage is enough. The sibling conjunct in that same All treats Medicare the same way, requiring ../enrolledInMedicareDerived to equal noneOfYear.
Whether the filer was eligible to make HSA contributions all year. Rule of last year does not apply.
The distributions associated with an HSA

Fact.Name: Some Form 1099-SA HSA distribution on this return paid qualified medical expenses
Fact.Description: True when /hsaDistributions is answered and at least one item has an answered ../writableQualifiedMedExpenses (the amount that item puts toward Form 8889 line 15) above $0. The per-item test is IsComplete-first, so an item whose qualified-expense answer is blank does not count, and the collection test is a Switch on IsComplete defaulting to false: a return that never reached the HSA distribution screens is Complete false. A selector for Schedule A, which must ask how much of its medical total an HSA paid (IRC 223(f)(6)); it does not measure that amount and computes no dollar figure.

Fact.Name: An Archer MSA or Medicare Advantage MSA distribution on this return paid qualified medical expenses
Fact.Description: True when Form 8853 line 7 (Archer MSA unreimbursed qualified medical expenses, /archerMsaForm8853Line7UnreimbursedQualifiedMedicalExpenses) is above $0, or when some filer's Form 8853 line 11 (Medicare Advantage MSA qualified medical expenses, /filers/*/medicareAdvantageMsaForm8853Line11QualifiedMedicalExpenses) is Complete and above $0. Both lines are complete-safe $0 when unanswered; the per-filer test is IsComplete-first and the count sits in a Switch on IsComplete(/filers) defaulting to false, so a return with no MSA is Complete false. A selector for Schedule A, which must ask how much of its medical total an MSA paid (IRC 220(f)(6); a Medicare Advantage MSA is an Archer MSA under IRC 138(b)); it computes no dollar figure.
The filer who the HSA distributions belong to.

Whether the filer is knocked out because one of their Form 1099-SA items carries a box 3 distribution code this dictionary does not admit, or no code at all. TRUE, on a return where some filer can have HSA distributions (/someFilerCanHaveDistribution), when an item's code is unanswered, or is answered and the item is none of: code 1, 2 or 3; an admitted code-4 surviving-spouse item (/hsaDistributions/*/isAdmittedSurvivingSpouseDeathDistribution); an admitted code-5 item (/hsaDistributions/*/isAdmittedProhibitedTransactionDistribution); an admitted code-4 or code-6 nonspouse-beneficiary item (/hsaDistributions/*/isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution); an admitted code-4 estate item on the decedent's own final return (/hsaDistributions/*/isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution).
CODE 2 is admitted with the return-of-excess machinery (/hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome).
CODE 3 (DISABILITY) IS ADMITTED because both halves of its statutory treatment ship on the ordinary collection route: the IRC 223(f)(2) inclusion is the printed line 16 chain (../taxableHsaDistributionTotal), and the IRC 223(f)(4)(B) forgiveness of the 20% additional tax is the attestation pair (../writableHsaCollectionExceptionAmount and ../writableHsaCollectionExceptionReason, whose options include disability). No silent overcharge is possible: a code-3 filer with a positive line 16 who has not answered the pair is refused by /flowKnockoutHsaUnqualifiedDistributions through ../causesUnattestedTaxableHsaDistributionKnockout, exactly as a code-1 filer is.
CODE 4, SURVIVING SPOUSE (the IRC 223(f)(8)(A) case ): under (A) the account is treated as if the spouse were the account beneficiary, so the item runs the ordinary chain exactly as a code-1 item does.
CODE 5 (PROHIBITED TRANSACTION) WITH THE JANUARY-1 VALUE ANSWERED BY THE ITEM'S OWNER. IRC 223(e)(2) makes the account cease to be an HSA and the deemed distribution is the January-1 fair market value of ALL the account's assets (i8889 "Deemed Distributions From HSAs"), an amount that is NOT box 1 of the Form 1099-SA. Its intake is /filers/*/writableHsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv, and a code-5 item whose OWNING FILER has answered it is admitted and runs the ordinary Part II chain with the January-1 value on line 14a (/filers/*/totalHsaDistributions), which is where the instructions put it and the only line they name.
CODE 6 OR CODE 4, NONSPOUSE BENEFICIARY: the recipient answered "filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary", with box 4 and the pre-death answer present. The pre-death qualified-expenses intake is /hsaDistributions/*/writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses, and the "separately marked beneficiary Form 8889" is a PRINT obligation rather than an arithmetic one - i8889 has the beneficiary complete Form 8889 with the date-of-death fair market value on line 14a and the pre-death expenses on line 15, and where the beneficiary also has an HSA of their own it has them file a statement form per account plus a CONTROLLING form "combining the amounts shown on each of the statement Forms 8889" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3). Per-filer aggregation IS that controlling form. i8889's "Death of Account Beneficiary" section keys on the beneficiary not being the surviving spouse and not on the box 3 code, so the same treatment covers the same beneficiary paid IN the year of death (code 4). The code-4 case carries no timing conflict: IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(II) puts the inclusion in the taxable year that includes the date of death, and a code-4 form is by its own definition the one issued for that year (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2), so the open owner question on the code-6 arm does not touch it.
CODE 4, ESTATE, ON THE DECEDENT'S OWN FINAL RETURN: a code-4 estate item admits where the item's owning filer is the one marked deceased on THIS return (/hsaDistributions/*/isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution argues the full population).
WHAT THIS GUARD'S COLLECTION ARM KEEPS, the complete list. FOUR are correct PERMANENT refusals and one is data completeness on the code itself; the clause letters are the ones the correct-refusal allowlist row cites: (a) the code-4 ESTATE case where this return is NOT the decedent's final return - an estate item belonging to a filer this return does not mark deceased, or on a return where nobody is marked deceased. i8889 (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3) names "the account beneficiary's final income tax return", and the estate's own Form 1099-SA carries the estate's TIN and reports to a return this dictionary does not file, so the refusal is correct and permanent. Measured both ways by review-r2-code4-estate-on-decedents-final-return (admitted) and hsa-death-code4-estate-still-refused (refused); (b) DATA COMPLETENESS on either death code - the recipient, box 4 or the pre-death expenses unanswered. The screens ship; the refused population shrinks with no dictionary edit as answers arrive. This is the one class REFUSAL-VERDICTS.md entitles to stand permanently; (c) the two RECIPIENT CONTRADICTIONS on a code-6 form (spouse, estate) and the two ROLLOVER/EXCESS CONTRADICTIONS on either code - document/answer conflicts no arithmetic can resolve, and refusing beats guessing which side of the conflict is true; (d) CODE 5 with no January-1 fair market value from the item's owner - completeness again, on a different intake (/filers/*/writableHsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv). It is the correct permanent refusal: without the figure the return would tax box 1 of the Form 1099-SA, a number IRC 408(e)(2)(B) does not use, instead of the whole account; (e) THE BOX-3 CODE ITSELF UNANSWERED. The Any(Not(IsComplete(code)), ...) arm refuses an unanswered code on its own, so an item entered without its code is never run through the ordinary Part II chain with box 1 taxed as though it were a normal (code-1) distribution - which would silently mistax a death (4/6) or prohibited-transaction (5) distribution. The screen makes the field REQUIRED; this is the dictionary half. Data completeness, correct permanently - the refused population shrinks with no dictionary edit once every filer answers box 3.
THE ROLLOVER/EXCESS CONTRADICTIONS in (c): an item answered YES to the box-1 rollover question (../writableDistributionsRolloverBool) or to the withdrawn-excess-contributions question (../hasWithdrawnExcessContributions). IRC 223(f)(5) admits a rollover only as a payment into a health savings account "of such beneficiary" and 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(I) ended the account on the date of death, so a nonspouse beneficiary can do neither. They are refused rather than ignored because printed line 14b subtracts from line 14a, and on an admitted item line 14a is the date-of-death fair market value - one YES answer would erase the entire inclusion on a return that FILES.
The FOUR measured GAPS the death treatment carries (no per-decedent aggregate cap, the one-directional clamp, post-death earnings, IRC 691(c)) are NOT refusals here and are carried in full by records /hsaDeathOfAccountBeneficiaryTreatment.

Knockout due to any of filers having an HSA distribution code the return cannot treat. Admitted: codes 1, 2 and 3; the code-4 surviving-spouse case (IRC 223(f)(8)(A), answered on /hsaDistributions/*/writableDeathDistributionRecipient); the code-4 and code-6 nonspouse-beneficiary case where the recipient, box 4 and the pre-death qualified-expenses intake are all answered (/hsaDistributions/*/isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution - IRC 223(f)(8)(B) keys on the beneficiary and not on the box-3 code); the code-4 estate case on the decedent's own final return; and code 5 with its January-1 value. The residue is the code-4 ESTATE case on any other return (the decedent's final return owns it), the completeness gaps on either death code, the recipient contradictions on a code-6 form, the rollover/withdrawn-excess contradictions on either, code 5 without its January-1 value, and an unanswered code. The per-filer term above records which machinery serves each admitted case and why the surviving refusals survive.

Fact.Name: Knockout due to distribution code not being normal distribution
Fact.Description:
User selects an HSA distribution code the return cannot treat - see /filers/*/hsaDistributionNotNormalKnockout for the admitted codes and cases, the switch that tells them apart and the grounds for each surviving refusal - OR attests a section 4975 prohibited transaction on the return-level Form 8889 attestation with no January-1 fair market value behind it. The collection arm stands on the correct-refusal allowlist (scripts/test_refusal_successor_allowlist.tsv); the code-4 estate case on a return that is not the decedent's final return is carried by records /hsaDeathOfAccountBeneficiaryTreatment through /flowKnockoutHsaDistributionFMV (the per-item term is /hsaDistributions/*/causesFmvKnockout).
THE SECOND ARM COVERS THE FILER WITH NO DOCUMENT. This module's collection intake /hsaDistributions carries a Box-3 distribution code whose enum includes prohibitedTransaction, and the collection arm reads it. A section 4975 prohibited transaction produces no Form 1099-SA, so a filer who has one is never asked a box-3 code; form8889 asks them instead, at the return level (/writableHsaProhibitedTransactionOccurred). form8889 /hasNonNormalTopLevelHsaDistribution is that attestation's complete-safe alias (FALSE when unanswered; "TopLevel" in its name means return-level, not per-1099-SA), precisely so that reading it here cannot take this fact, and through it flow /flowIsKnockedOut, Incomplete by contagion.
THE PLEDGE LEG IS NOT HERE. The other deemed-distribution situation (an HSA used as security for a loan) routes to /flowKnockoutHsaDistributionFMV instead, because it turns on a fair market value rather than on a distribution code. Wiring one Boolean into both knockouts would make a pledge case trip this code knockout, which is semantically wrong even where the refusal outcome is the same.
THE SECOND ARM REFUSES ONLY while NO filer has answered the January-1 fair market value (/someFilerAnsweredHsaDeemedDistributionJanuary1Fmv). Answered, the amount lands on that filer's Form 8889 line 14a and the return computes.
WHY THE RETURN-LEVEL ARM USES A RETURN-LEVEL TEST while the collection arm uses a per-owner one. The attestation itself is return-level, by the design the module header of dictionary/ty2025/form8889.xml records: a section 4975 prohibited transaction produces no Form 1099-SA, so there is no document to attribute and no per-filer answer to key on. The sharpest question that can be asked of it is therefore "has SOMEBODY on this return supplied the amount". The per-item arm, which does have an owner, asks the sharper question.
THE RESIDUE THIS KEEPS, NAMED: a return-level section 4975 attestation with no filer's January-1 value behind it. Data completeness, permanent, and the same residue in kind as the collection arm's.
AND TWO THIS ARM CANNOT CATCH, NAMED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE FOUND. On a joint return where BOTH spouses have HSAs, the attestation says a section 4975 prohibited transaction happened somewhere on this return but not WHOSE account it was - it cannot, being return-level.
(i) IF THE WRONG SPOUSE ANSWERS, the amount lands on THAT spouse's Form 8889 line 14a and the return files. Measured on an MFJ probe: a filer who owns no code-5 document carried ../totalHsaDistributions of $12,000 purely because they typed the value. The return-level TOTALS are right (Schedule 1 line 8f and Schedule 2 line 17c sum both spouses' forms); what is wrong is which of the two attached Forms 8889 carries them, and on a return where the two spouses' Part II figures differ - different qualified expenses on line 15, different exception attestations - the totals can move as well, because line 16 is computed per filer before it is summed.
(ii) IF BOTH SPOUSES ANSWER, ONE EVENT IS REPORTED TWICE and the guard RELEASES. The trigger /hsaDeemedDistributionSection4975Triggered is return-level, so it opens the question for every filer and nothing in the graph can say the second answer is the same event as the first. Measured on the MFJ fixture named below with the PRIMARY's answer added as well: both spouses answering $12,000 against one $12,000 event gives /flowKnockoutHsaDistributionCode FALSE (the guard RELEASES, because the owner has answered), the primary's line 14a $20,000 (box 1 $8,000 plus $12,000) and the secondary's $12,000, and /hsaCollectionRouteTaxableDistributions $30,000 against the $18,000 the same return produces when only the owner answers. THE DOLLARS ARE WRONG WHEN THAT HAPPENS - one deemed distribution is included twice - and the direction is taxpayer-ADVERSE (double inclusion, double 20% tax).
Both are data-CONSISTENCY defects, not data-completeness ones - the filer chose a spouse, or answered twice - and no graph test can distinguish either, because the graph holds no per-account ownership for an event that produces no document. A count-based gate was considered and REFUSED: two spouses can each have had a prohibited transaction on their own account, so refusing a second answer would refuse a legitimate return. They are therefore SCREEN-WORDING obligations ("ask the spouse whose account it was, and ask it once per account, not once per spouse"). Recorded here so the guard is not later widened in the belief that it was an oversight.
