Fact.Name: Who received this death-code HSA distribution
Fact.Description: Who received the distribution this death-code Form 1099-SA (box 3 code 4 or 6) reports: the decedent's surviving spouse designated beneficiary, the decedent's estate, or this filer as a nonspouse designated beneficiary. The 1099-SA itself does not carry this fact - code 4 covers BOTH the estate (any year) and any beneficiary paid in the year of death - so the recipient must be asked before the module can pick between IRC 223(f)(8)(A) and 223(f)(8)(B). On a code-4 form this answer is the WHOLE DISCRIMINATOR, because IRC 223(f)(8)(B) and i8889 "Death of Account Beneficiary" key on the beneficiary and never on the box-3 code: "surviving spouse" routes to IRC 223(f)(8)(A) and the ordinary chain; "this filer as nonspouse beneficiary", beside box 4 and ../writableDecedentPredeathQualifiedMedExpenses, routes to the 223(f)(8)(B) inclusion (box 4 to line 14a, the clamped pre-death expenses to line 15, no 20% tax), on a code-4 or a code-6 form alike; "estate" routes to the decedent's own final return - ../isAdmittedEstateDeathDistribution admits the item only when its owning filer is the one marked deceased on this return - and refuses otherwise. On a code-6 form "surviving spouse" and "estate" are both document/answer contradictions and refuse. SCREEN CONSEQUENCE FOR the application: this screen is also the GATE of the pre-death-expenses question, which the application shows on the same screen, and that question is gated by the ANSWER and not by the code - show it whenever this answer is "filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary", on a code-4 form as well as a code-6 one. A the application screen asks it only where a death code is present (grouped writables); unanswered, it leaves ../isAdmittedSurvivingSpouseDeathDistribution complete-safe FALSE and the death-code refusal stands.

Fact.Name: The decedent's pre-death qualified medical expenses this beneficiary paid within one year of the death
Fact.Description:
The IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduction, and the amount the beneficiary's Form 8889 line 15 carries on a death-code Form 1099-SA admitted through ../isAdmittedNonspouseBeneficiaryDeathDistribution. It is asked on EITHER death code, because the statute keys the reduction to who acquired the interest and not to the box-3 code.
SCREEN SPECIFICATION (the application builds this screen from this Description without opening an IRS document).
THE QUESTION: "How much of the deceased account holder's own medical expenses did you pay within one year after their death?"
HELP TEXT: "When you inherit someone's health savings account and you are not their spouse, the account stops being an HSA on the day they died and its value on that day counts as your income. You can subtract from that income any qualified medical expenses the deceased person ran up BEFORE they died, as long as YOU paid them within one year after the date of death. Enter the total of those payments. [[CODE-CONDITIONAL SENTENCE - THE APPLICATION MUST BRANCH HERE, and the branch is one boolean. SHOW the next sentence ONLY when ../isDeathDistributionToNonspouseAfterYearOfDeath is TRUE (box 3 code 6; the fact ships with ). When ../isDeathDistributionOtherThanCode6 is TRUE (box 3 code 4; also exported), SHOW INSTEAD: "Include the deceased person's own pre-death medical bills you paid within a year of the death, whether you paid them out of your own pocket or out of the inherited account." WHY, in one line: the trustee nets those payments out of box 4 on the AFTER-year form only (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2 continuing at 64-65) and NOT on the year-of-death form (line 115), so shipping the code-6 sentence on a code-4 item under-states line 15 and over-states line 16 - taxpayer-ADVERSE. The full argument is under "WHAT A CODE-4 ITEM CHANGES ON THIS SCREEN" at the end of this Description.]] Do not include anything paid out of the HSA itself - the account's trustee has already subtracted those from box 4 of your Form 1099-SA. [[END CODE-CONDITIONAL SENTENCE.]] Do not include your own medical expenses, and do not include expenses the deceased person incurred after the date of death. If you inherited more than one HSA from the SAME person, split that person's pre-death expenses across those forms - do not enter the full total on each." (Paraphrasing IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I), 26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024, "shall be reduced by the amount of qualified medical expenses which were incurred by the decedent before the date of the decedent's death and paid by such person within 1 year after such date"; and the 2025 Instructions for Form 8889, "Death of Account Beneficiary", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3, "On Part II, line 15, for a beneficiary other than the estate, enter qualified medical expenses incurred by the account beneficiary before the date of death that the beneficiary paid within 1 year after the date of death". The "not out of the HSA itself" sentence is the 2025 Instructions for Forms 1099-SA and 5498-SA box 4 rule, which nets exactly those payments out of box 4 before the beneficiary ever sees it: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2 continuing at lines 64-65, "Box 4, the FMV of the account on the date of death, reduced by any payments from the HSA made for the decedent's qualified medical expenses, if paid within 1 year after death".)
ASKED WHEN: on a /hsaDistributions item whose box 3 (../hsaDistributionCode) is EITHER DEATH CODE - code 4, "4-Death distribution other than code 6", or code 6, "6-Death distribution after year of death to a nonspouse beneficiary" - AND whose recipient answer ../writableDeathDistributionRecipient is "filerAsNonspouseBeneficiary" - i.e. the beneficiary is a filer of THIS return. The RECIPIENT ANSWER is the gate, not the code: IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduces the inclusion of "any person (other than the estate)" who acquired the interest and never mentions the box-3 code, and the 1099-SA instructions give the same beneficiary's payment code 4 when the trustee pays it IN the year of death and code 6 when after (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2). One answer per Form 1099-SA, on the same screen as the recipient question, because the i8889 Note at https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3 makes the beneficiary Form 8889 a PER-ACCOUNT form ("If, during the tax year, you are the beneficiary of two or more HSAs ... you must complete a separate Form 8889 for each HSA"), and the collection item is this dictionary's per-account unit. Never asked on any NON-death box 3 code (1, 2, 3 or 5), and never asked where the recipient is the surviving spouse or the estate.
UNANSWERED POSTURE: REFUSED. hsa:/flowKnockoutHsaDistributionCode keeps the return until this question is answered, because the (B)(i) inclusion cannot be reduced by an unknown: computing without it would put the WHOLE date-of-death fair market value into gross income, which is taxpayer-ADVERSE, and defaulting it to 0 would silently assert that the beneficiary paid none of the decedent's expenses. An answer of 0 is a real answer and is the right one for a beneficiary who paid nothing; it is the MISSING answer that refuses.
VALIDATION: Dollar, Min $0, no Max, no default. There is no upper limit on the SCREEN because the decedent's pre-death expenses can genuinely exceed the account's value; the graph clamps the line-15 contribution at the item's own box 4 instead (see ../form8889Line15ItemAmount), because IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduces "the amount includible in gross income under clause (i)" and a reduction cannot take that inclusion below zero. the application should NOT show a validation error when the answer exceeds box 4.
WHAT THE ANSWER FEEDS: ../form8889Line15ItemAmount (printed Form 8889 line 15, clamped at box 4), hence /filers/*/taxableHsaDistributionTotal (line 16) and Schedule 1 line 8f; and ../deathBeneficiaryInclusionAmount, which carries the same amount into /filers/*/hsaAdditionalTaxExceptionAmountDerived so that the death inclusion bears NO 20% additional tax (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf, page 3, "The distribution is not subject to the additional 20% tax").
NOT ASKED, AND NAMED SO THE APPLICATION DOES NOT INVENT IT: the ordinary line-15 question ../writableQualifiedMedExpenses is NOT asked on an admitted death item of EITHER code. The beneficiary's Form 8889 line 15 is the pre-death expenses and nothing else, by the i8889 bullet cited above.
THE ALLOCATION RULE AND ITS RESIDUE. The reduction is scoped PER PERSON PER DECEDENT and not per account: IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(ii)(I) reduces the inclusion "by any person (other than the estate)" by the decedent's expenses that person paid (26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024), while clause (i) generates one inclusion per account ACQUIRED. The per-item clamp in ../form8889Line15ItemAmount reproduces that granularity exactly when the beneficiary inherited ONE account from that decedent, and only then. This dictionary holds no decedent identity, so the split is the filer's to make and the screen says so, in the help text's "If you inherited more than one HSA from the SAME person, split that person's pre-death expenses across those forms" sentence. THE RESIDUE, NAMED AND NOT BUILT: there is NO per-decedent aggregate cap in the graph. A filer who ignores the instruction and enters the same $8,000 of one decedent's expenses on two inherited accounts gets $16,000 of reduction against $8,000 of real expenses (measured: line 16 $2,000 where the statute gives $10,000, taxpayer-FAVOURABLE); the mirror filer who puts the whole amount against one account loses a reduction the statute allows. Building the cap needs a decedent identifier on /hsaDistributions, which is a separate intake and a separate unit. Until it exists this intake and ../form8889Line15ItemAmount stay interpretation:provisional.
THE YEAR-OF-DEATH DISCLOSURE, and it is the screen's job because the graph cannot see the year. TWO SOURCES PUT THIS INCLUSION IN THE YEAR OF DEATH, not in the year of the Form 1099-SA. IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(II) includes the date-of-death fair market value in the acquirer's gross income "for the taxable year which includes such date" (26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024). Publication 969, "Death of HSA Holder", says the same to the taxpayer in its two bullets for a designated beneficiary who is not the spouse: https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p969.pdf, page 10 ("The account stops being an HSA") and, of the fair market value, ("the beneficiary in the year in which you die") - a two-column extraction whose right column interleaves at line 641 and whose sentence completes at line 643. A box-3 CODE 6 is BY ITS OWN DEFINITION issued after the year of death (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 3), so computing a code-6 item on THIS return - the return the code-6 document arrives with - knowingly puts the inclusion in a later year than the statute names. i8889's beneficiary section is silent on the year, which is the only support the form reading has.
THAT DEFECT IS PERMANENT FOR A CODE-6 ITEM AND THAT IS WHY THE ITEM IS COMPUTED RATHER THAN REFUSED. Because a code-6 form is by definition issued after the year of death, no TY2025 return can EVER be the statutorily correct return for a code-6 item: a code-6 form processed here necessarily reports a death in 2024 or earlier. Refusing the item would therefore not defer it to the right year - it would re-refuse the entire nonspouse-beneficiary population, permanently, for a defect that the disclosure below states plainly instead of hiding. The residue is the intake that would let the graph route rather than disclose: a date-of-death or year-of-death fact on /hsaDistributions, which is a separate unit and outside what a single-tax-year engine holds today.
THE SENTENCE THE APPLICATION MUST SHOW BESIDE THIS QUESTION, verbatim: [[CODE-CONDITIONAL - SHOW ON CODE 6 ONLY, and show NOTHING in its place on code 4. The branch is the same one boolean as the help-text sentence above: show this only when ../isDeathDistributionToNonspouseAfterYearOfDeath is TRUE; when ../isDeathDistributionOtherThanCode6 is TRUE (box 3 code 4) SUPPRESS it entirely. Both facts carry an Export of their downstream facts. WHY: a code-4 form IS the year-of-death form (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2), so the return it arrives with IS the taxable year IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(II) names and this sentence would tell the filer to amend the return they are sitting on.]] "The law puts this amount in the year the account holder died. If you already reported this account's date-of-death value on the return for that year, do not report it again here - amend that return instead." [[END CODE-CONDITIONAL.]] Without it a compliant taxpayer who followed Pub. 969 is taxed on the same dollars TWICE, which is a wrong number and not a conservatism.
WHAT A CODE-4 ITEM CHANGES ON THIS SCREEN, and both changes are conditional on the box-3 code of the item being asked about; neither moves a dollar the graph computes.
(1) THE YEAR-OF-DEATH DISCLOSURE IS A CODE-6 SENTENCE AND MUST NOT BE SHOWN ON A CODE-4 ITEM. The two paragraphs above are entirely correct for code 6 and entirely INAPPLICABLE to code 4: a code-4 death distribution is by the 1099-SA instructions' own definition the one the trustee pays "in the year of death" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2), so the return it arrives with IS "the taxable year which includes such date" that IRC 223(f)(8)(B)(i)(II) names (26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024). There is no gap between the statute's year and the form's year and no double-inclusion risk. Showing "The law puts this amount in the year the account holder died ... amend that return instead" beside a code-4 question would tell a filer to amend the very return they are sitting on. SHOW IT ON CODE 6 ONLY.
(2) THE BOX-4 NETTING SENTENCE IN THE HELP TEXT IS ALSO CODE-6 ONLY, AND ON A CODE-4 ITEM IT IS FALSE IN THE TAXPAYER-ADVERSE DIRECTION. The help text's "Do not include anything paid out of the HSA itself - the account's trustee has already subtracted those from box 4 of your Form 1099-SA" is the AFTER-year rule and only the after-year rule: the 1099-SA instructions tell the trustee to report, for a distribution after the year of death, "Box 4, the FMV of the account on the date of death, reduced by any payments from the HSA made for the decedent's qualified medical expenses, if paid within 1 year after death" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-prior/i1099sa--2025.pdf, page 2 continuing at lines 64-65), while for a distribution IN the year of death the same instructions say only "Box 4, the FMV of the account on the date of death" (line 115) with NO reduction clause. So on a code-4 form box 4 is the GROSS date-of-death value, the trustee has netted nothing, and a filer told to exclude HSA-paid amounts would under-state line 15 and over-state line 16 - adverse. THE SENTENCE THE APPLICATION MUST SHOW INSTEAD, on a code-4 item: "Include the deceased person's own pre-death medical bills you paid within a year of the death, whether you paid them out of your own pocket or out of the inherited account." NOTHING IN THE GRAPH CHANGES: both codes read the same intake and the same ../form8889Line15ItemAmount clamp, and the difference is entirely in what the filer should count. The residue is that the graph cannot verify the filer applied the right rule - the same class of screen-wording obligation as the per-decedent split above, and taxpayer-FAVOURABLE only if the filer over-counts.

Total amount of qualified medical expenses paid for in the tax year using distributions from this HSA account. Informs Form 8889 line 15.
Help text: "qualified medical expenses" means unreimbursed medical care costs, within the meaning of IRC section 213(d), that are not compensated by insurance or otherwise. HEALTH INSURANCE PREMIUMS DO NOT COUNT, with four exceptions: (1) a COBRA-type continuation- coverage premium required by federal law; (2) a qualified long-term-care insurance premium; (3) a health-plan premium paid while you are receiving unemployment compensation under federal or state law; or (4) if you have reached Medicare eligibility age, any health insurance premium OTHER THAN a Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policy. Every other insurance premium — ordinary health insurance, dental or vision premiums, and Medigap — is NOT a qualified medical expense even though paid from the HSA, and belongs on line 16 as a taxable distribution instead. This module cannot classify what a distribution was spent on; the total you enter here is trusted as the qualified portion, so leaving a premium in it understates line 16 and the 20% additional tax with it.

Fact.Name: Secondary filer has HSA distribution Form 8889 when primary filer is not filing jointly
Fact.Description:
Whether secondary filer has HSA distribution records when primary filer is not filing jointly
COMPLETENESS SHAPE. The Derived All opens with IsComplete(filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ) and IsComplete(filers:/secondaryFiler), ahead of the guard's own operands, the shape every module carrying this guard shares. WHY THE CLASS NEEDS IT, and why THIS module does not: in most modules carrying this guard, ../belongsToSecondaryFiler compares ../filer with filers:/secondaryFiler, and on a SINGLE-FILER return /secondaryFiler is a Find that resolves to nothing - so without the conjuncts the guard, the collection guard's Count(...) > 0 and everything reading them would be Incomplete, and the knockout could not be shown false. THIS module is NOT one of those: /hsaDistributions/*/belongsToSecondaryFiler is Not(Equal(../filer, filers:/primaryFiler)), and /primaryFiler always exists, so it is Complete whenever ../filer is answered and this guard resolves Complete false on a single-filer return either way. The conjuncts are here for class uniformity and for the unanswered-/filingStatus edge; against the corpus they are a behavioural no-op. NO REFUSAL MOVES ON THEM: All short-circuits on a Complete-false operand, so the only transition is Incomplete -> Complete false. LEFT ALONE ON PURPOSE: an unanswered ../filer on a TWO-FILER non-MFJ return stays Incomplete, because filers:/secondaryFiler is Complete there - which is why the conjunct is IsComplete(filers:/secondaryFiler) and not IsComplete(../belongsToSecondaryFiler). This module carries the divergent third operand /someFilerCanHaveDistribution. It is also the only guard in the class read by a Not() elsewhere (/hsaDistributions/*/hasDistributionsWithoutHsaActivity), which cannot widen because that fact's sibling IsComplete(../filer/hasHsaCanHaveDistribution) conjunct short-circuits an unanswered ../filer.

Whether the filer had distributions as form 8889 listed after claiming they had no HSA activity.
NO "SOMEONE CAN HAVE DISTRIBUTIONS" OPERAND, DELIBERATELY. A first All operand /someFilerCanHaveDistribution, resting on the premise "We only display the distribution section if someone could have distributions so only need to alert if some filer can have distributions", would make this guard INERT in exactly the state where it is needed most, and the inertness would be a SILENT UNDERSTATEMENT of income:
* When that operand held, one filer of two could not have distributions and the other could, so a distribution attributed to the first would be caught here. * When it did NOT hold, NO filer could have distributions, so EVERY entered Form 1099-SA would hit the same drop and nothing would catch any of them. ../filer/hasHsaCanHaveDistribution false takes /filers/*/ taxableHsaDistributionTotal to Incomplete (its Switch has no default Case, by the deliberate choice recorded on that fact), so ../taxableHsaDistributionTotalOrZero falls to its Dollar 0 branch and Schedule 1 line 8f sums a zero. The return would then FILE, with the taxable distribution missing.
THAT SWITCH IS NOT THE DEFECT AND IS NOT TOUCHED. A filer who genuinely cannot have an HSA distribution has no Form 8889 line 16, and a 0 term on line 8f is the correct rendering of "no Form 8889"; giving that Switch a True-arm 0 would flip every non-HSA filer Incomplete to Complete 0 for no tax reason. What must not happen is that a return carrying a Form 1099-SA reaches that state and files. This fact IS the refusal of that contradiction, rather than a line 16 computed out of answers the filer never gave: the whole coverage and contribution section is skipped for a filer who cannot have distributions, so the line 14c input the computation would need rests on nothing.
A SERVICE-SIDE PREMISE CANNOT CARRY A FACT-GRAPH GUARD. "We only display the distribution section if…" is a claim about the interview screens, which invariant #7 puts in another repo. Nothing in this dictionary stops /hsaDistributions from carrying an item while /someFilerHadNonW2HsaActivity is answered false — and the ordinary way a filer gets there is by answering the activity question AFTER entering the form, or by editing the answer later, which is the same stale-state class the eight /*/secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ guards exist for.
WHAT DOES NOT FIRE, so the guard is not read as wider than it is: the IsComplete operand below keeps the guard silent while ../filer/ hasHsaCanHaveDistribution is Incomplete, which is the mid-interview state of a filer who has entered a Form 1099-SA and not yet answered the activity question — refusing there would refuse everyone in the middle of the section. And a filer with a box-12 code W on their W-2 has HSA activity whatever they answer to the non-W2 question, so the combat-pay shape (scenarios/upstream/mfj-cdcc-combat-pay-2024-verified) is untouched. Pinned by node tests of a no-activity answer with a Form 1099-SA (blocked), employer HSA contributions on a W-2 (still computes) and an unanswered activity question (complete-safe).
A DISTRIBUTION-ONLY FILER IS NOT SWEPT IN, and this is the population it would be easiest to break: someone who contributed nothing this year and only spent the account down answers YES to the activity question, and their line 16 computes. The shipping tests/nodes/ty2025/form8889/hsa-collection-distribution-code-normal-computes is exactly that filer (writablePrimaryFilerHasMadeContributionsToHsa false, a 8,000 gross distribution against 2,000 of qualified expenses) and it resolves line 16 at 6,000.

Whether the TP has any distributions that must be removed because they reported not having HSA activity in the TY
The return-level projection of /hsaDistributions/*/hasDistributionsWithoutHsaActivity, and the tag-bearing half of the pair - the per-item leg states the contradiction, this fact carries the BlockSubmissionOnTrue that acts on it. The authority comment below is the per-item leg's own, repeated here rather than left to be inferred from a sibling.

Fact.Name: Community-property allocated HSA distributions (Form 8958 line 12) — $0, a disclosed non-allocation
Fact.Description:
THE CONTRACT PATH, and it resolves $0 on every return including a community property allocation return. It is the amount this return ALLOCATES under Form 8958 line 12 for HSA distributions — the amount that CROSSES between columns B and C — and that amount is ZERO.
IT IS NOT THE FORM 8958 LINE 12 COLUMN B FIGURE, and the distinction is the one the social security sibling had to be corrected on. Column A of a Form 8958 row carries the item's WHOLE amount, separate income included (" Enter the total amount of your community or separate income," / "deductions, credits, and other return amounts on their respective" / "lines in column A. Enter each spouse’s or RDP’s allocation of these", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8958.pdf, page 4, LEFT column of a two column extraction), and columns B and C must sum back to it ("amounts in columns B and C. Together, columns B and C should" / "equal column A.", lines 201-202, LEFT column). On the reading below each spouse's taxable HSA distribution is that spouse's own for federal purposes, so this taxpayer's column B for the row is ALL of their own distributions and column C is all of the spouse's. ZERO is the amount that crosses, which is what this fact states and is the only figure the allocation itself produces.
WHY, AND THIS ROW'S ARGUMENT IS A STATUTORY ONE RATHER THAN AN ABSENCE — which is what separates it from its social security sibling and from the contract's own expectation. (1) Form 8958 line 12 is the line for items the form does NOT characterise: "Identify any item not previously reported, such as social security" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8958.pdf, page 4, RIGHT column of a two column extraction), and the form hands the character question to the filer and to state law, "You and your spouse or RDP must be able to identify your" community and separate income (line 147, LEFT column). Neither Form 8958 nor Publication 555 nor Publication 969 nor the Form 8889 instructions say anything about health savings accounts and community property: greps for "health savings", "HSA", "Archer" and "medical savings" over https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8958.pdf and https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p555.pdf, and for "community" over https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p969.pdf, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i8889.pdf and https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f8889.pdf, were each run to completion and return nothing on point. (2) THE CODE DOES SAY IT, DIRECTLY AND WITHOUT AN ANALOGY. IRC 223(d)(4) reads "Rules similar to the following rules shall" / "apply for purposes of this section:" and its subparagraph (D) is "(D) Section 408(g) (relating to community" / "property laws)." (26 U.S.C. 223, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section223&num=0&edition=2024, RIGHT column of a two column extraction). IRC 408(g) reads "This section shall be applied without regard to" / "any community property laws." (26 U.S.C. 408, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section408&num=0&edition=2024, LEFT column). "This section" in the incorporating clause is section 223 ENTIRE, which contains the two provisions this module computes: IRC 223(f)(2), "health savings account which is not used ex-" / "penses of the account beneficiary shall be in-" / "cluded in the gross income of such beneficiary." (lines 341-344, LEFT column), i.e. Form 8889 line 16 into Schedule 1 line 8f; and IRC 223(f)(4)(A), "The tax imposed by this chapter on the ac-" / "count beneficiary for any taxable year in" / "which there is a payment or distribution" / "from a health savings account of such bene-" / "ficiary which is includible in gross income" / "under paragraph (2) shall be increased by 20" / "percent of the amount which is so includible." (lines 385-391, LEFT column), i.e. Form 8889 line 17b into Schedule 2 line 17c. Both figures are therefore computed without regard to community property law, and there is nothing for Form 8958 to move.
THIS IS THE AUTHORITY THE CONTRACT ASKED FOR, AND IT IS NOT THE IRA ANALOGY THE CONTRACT FORBADE. The contract's NAMED AUTHORITY GAP said a fill owes "either an authority that reaches HSAs or an explicit disclosure that it is extending the IRA rule by analogy". IRC 223(d)(4)(D) is the former. Form 8958's IRA paragraph — "Withdrawals from individual retirement arrangements (IRAs)." / "There are several kinds of IRAs. Distributions of IRAs by law are" / "deemed to be separate property, even if the funds in the account" (lines 164-166, LEFT column) — is CORROBORATION and not the ground: it is the IRS's own printed reading of the very provision, section 408(g), that section 223 incorporates. Nothing here reasons from IRAs to HSAs; the two share one statutory rule and the form states the outcome for the one the form happens to name.
WHAT THIS FACT DOES NOT CLAIM. It does not claim that a state's community property law is irrelevant to who OWNS an HSA balance, nor that the divorce transfer rule of IRC 223(f)(7) is affected; it claims only that section 223's own INCLUSION and ADDITIONAL TAX are applied without regard to community property law, which is what an allocation of the printed line would have had to overcome. It does not claim that Publication 555's silence proves anything; the silence is reported, and the statute is the ground.
NO CHARACTER WRITABLE IS ADDED FOR THIS COLLECTION, deliberately, and this is where the row parts company with interest, dividends and unemployment. Those three added a per item "is this community income?" attestation because no source characterises their items either way and the filer's answer under state law is the only available one. Here a federal rule disapplies state law for the computation, so a writable would invite a filer to attest a character that cannot change the figure.
THE GUARD DOES NOT NARROW. /hsaDistributions/secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ keeps its entire current scope — a spouse's Form 1099-SA on a non joint return is still an input contradiction with no line to sit on, and on this reading it is one on a community property allocation return too.

Form 8889 Line 13: The total deductible amount based off the filer's HSA coverage and contributions.
Complete when the filer hasMadeContributionsToHsa, or when Form 8889 Part I is owed for a prior-year carry-in (the third Case below).
LINE 13 HAS TWO TERMS. The second is the i5329 line 43 instruction's second half - an absorbed prior-year excess becomes deductible this year - and it is the smaller of Form 5329 line 43 and the excess of line 42 over line 44. Without it a filer whose carry-in was absorbed would pay the right 6% excise and take too small a deduction, taxpayer-ADVERSE. Measured on a Part VII carry-in return: line 13 $2,150.00 rather than $2,000.00, with line 46 and the excise unmoved at $1,850.00 and $111.00. The addend cannot take this fact Incomplete - lines 42, 43 and 44 each carry a True default arm - and it is $0 for every filer with no carry-in.
THIRD CASE: THE CARRY-IN-ONLY FILER. A filer who made no 2025 contributions but reports a Form 5329 line 42 prior-year excess is owed Form 8889 Part I (../hsaForm8889PartIRequired), so line 12 and Form 5329 line 43 compute for them, and line 13 is the absorbed deduction alone: the smaller of line 43 and the excess, if any, of line 42 over line 44. The dependent denial above reads the same Part I gate, so a carry-in-only filer another taxpayer may claim still deducts nothing.

Fact.Name: The filer's coverage-and-contributions section is complete AND their HSA contributions exceed the computed limit
Fact.Description: True once this filer's Form 8889 coverage-and-contributions section is fully answered AND their total HSA contributions exceed the limit computed from it. THIS FACT DOES NOT BLOCK SUBMISSION BY ITSELF - it is a shared gate, not a knockout: it feeds the two HSA-contributions-summary-table overage visibility facts (so the interview shows the overage to every over-limit filer), the Form 5329 line 47 excess-contributions gross (../hsaForm5329Line47CurrentYearExcess), and the employer-excess-income candidate (../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled). Submission is refused only where one of those downstream facts' own BlockSubmissionOnTrue fires (today, /flowHsaContributionsOverLimitKnockout's narrower Form 8889 line 10 funding-distribution overflow slice, and ../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled's own residual); an ordinary own-contribution excess reads this fact true and still files, with its 6% excise computed at ../hsaForm5329Line47CurrentYearExcess.

Fact.Name: An over-limit HSA return whose line 10 funding distribution overflows onto a line this dictionary cannot reach
Fact.Description:
Refuses a return on which a filer's Form 8889 line 10 qualified HSA funding distribution ALONE exceeds their line 8 limitation and the IRC 408(d)(9)(C)(i) exclusion cap cannot be computed: the Any runs over the per-filer arm /filers/*/causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled.
WHAT FILES. An over-limit filer's excess contribution is computed: Form 5329 Part VII computes at /hsaExcessContributionExciseTaxForm5329PartVii and reaches Schedule 2 line 8, so an OWN-contribution excess - the ordinary case - files with its 6% tax. A filer whose employer contributions and funding distributions (Form 8889 line 11) exceed their line 8 limitation owes an "Other income" add-back, and it ships at /hsaSchedule1Line8zEmployerExcessOtherIncome, consumed by income:/schedule1TotalOtherIncome (Schedule 1 line 8z), with its intake at /writableHsaEmployerExcessAlreadyInW2Income routed as An employer excess FILES with the income on the return.
WHAT IT REFUSES is a narrow slice on a printed LINE - not a missing amount and not a missing tax. Where the filer's Form 8889 line 10 qualified HSA funding distribution ALONE exceeds their line 8 limitation, the excess overflows line 9 and stops being an employer contribution; IRC 408(d)(9)(C)(i) caps the funding distribution's exclusion at the section 223(b) limitation computed at the time of the transfer, so the overflow is includible as an IRA DISTRIBUTION on Form 1040 line 4b rather than as compensation on Schedule 1 line 8z, and the (C)(i) cap is not the prorated line 8 this dictionary holds. Where the cap computes (/filers/*/hsaFundingDistributionExclusionCapComputable) the overflow goes to Form 1040 line 4b and the return files; what refuses is an overflow whose cap cannot be computed - no monthly coverage vector, or the transfer month unanswered. The whole of that is argued on /filers/*/causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled.
../hsaContributionsOverLimitAndComplete feeds /flowHsaContributionsSummaryTableOverageVisibility and its spouse twin, so every over-limit filer sees the overage in the interview; only the slice above BLOCKS.
Whether the HSA contributions summary table overage should be visible
Whether the HSA contributions summary table overage should be visible

Fact.Name: This 1099-SA's timely-returned excess CONTRIBUTIONS, with the earnings taken back out
Fact.Description:
../withdrawnExcessContributionsAmount MINUS ../earningsOnExcessContributionsOrZero, floored at zero.
WHY THE SUBTRACTION EXISTS. ../withdrawnExcessContributionsAmount is Form 8889 line 14b's per-item share and its own Description says so in as many words: "Amount of excess contributions and earnings on them withdrawn before the end of the tax year". Line 14b agrees - it carries "any excess contributions (and the earnings on those excess contributions) included on line 14a that were withdrawn by the due date of your return". Form 5329 line 47, by contrast, reduces the excess by the CONTRIBUTIONS treated as not having been made; the earnings are not a contribution and are taxed instead as income under IRC 223(f)(3)(A), on /hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome. Subtracting the gross line-14b figure would remove the earnings from the excise base as well, understating the tax by 6% of the earnings on every partial return - silently, and in the taxpayer-favourable direction. The fixture hsa-5329-partvii-partial-withdrawal-with-earnings pins the difference.
THE FLOOR IS PER ITEM, not per filer, so a distribution reporting earnings without a withdrawal cannot net against a different distribution's returned contributions.
COMPLETE-SAFE: both operands are complete-safe $0.

The primary filer's timely-returned excess CONTRIBUTIONS, earnings excluded. Mirrors the shape of /primaryFilerWithdrawnExcessContributionsAmount, which is the same sum over the gross line-14b figure.
The secondary filer's timely-returned excess CONTRIBUTIONS, earnings excluded.

Fact.Name: This filer's timely-returned excess CONTRIBUTIONS, earnings excluded
Fact.Description: The amount Form 5329 line 47 subtracts as "treated as not having been contributed". It is ../hsaTotalExcessContributionsWithdrawnInTime with the box-2 earnings removed; the selection between the two filers' collections is byte-identical in shape to that fact, which is the gross line-14b figure.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 42 - this filer's prior-year excess HSA contributions
Fact.Description:
The amount from line 48 of this filer's 2024 Form 5329, entered on their 2025 Form 5329 line 42 - the excess contributions that were still in the HSA at the end of 2024 and are therefore carried into 2025. The instruction conditions the entry on the prior year's tax having been owed: "Enter the amount from line 48 of your 2024 Form 5329 only if the amount on line 49 of your 2024 Form 5329 is more than zero", so a filer whose 2024 line 49 was zero enters nothing here.
THIS IS A TAXPAYER ATTESTATION FROM A PRIOR-YEAR RETURN, not something this dictionary can derive: nothing in a TY2025 return carries a TY2024 Form 5329.
UNANSWERED IS REFUSED, NOT DEFAULTED, and the direction is the reason. The return already asks /writableHasHsaExcessContributionsPreviousYear, so a filer can say "yes, I have one" and supply no amount. Treating that as $0 would file the return with the 6% tax silently OMITTED - understated tax, invisible to the filer. /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions keeps refusing exactly that slice instead.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 49 - the value of this filer's HSAs on December 31, 2025
Fact.Description:
The value of this filer's HSAs on December 31, 2025, including 2025 contributions made in 2026. Line 49 taxes 6% of the SMALLER of line 48 and this value, so it can only ever REDUCE the tax: it is the relief for a filer whose account has fallen below the excess still sitting in it.
REQUIRED WHENEVER THIS FILER'S FORM 5329 LINE 48 IS POSITIVE. IRC 4973(a)'s flush text and the line 49 instruction both phrase the smaller-of as mandatory, not elective, so an excess with no value supplied refuses the return (../causesHsaForm5329Line49AccountValueUnsupplied, gating the STANDALONE /flowKnockoutHsaForm5329Line49AccountValueUnsupplied - see that fact for why it is not a slice of /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions) rather than defaulting to the unbounded, larger figure.

Fact.Name: Whether this filer has supplied their Form 5329 line 42 carry-in amount
Fact.Description: Answeredness only, with no view on the amount: true once ../writableHsaPriorYearExcessContributionsForm5329Line48 resolves, including when it resolves to $0 (a filer whose 2024 line 49 was zero enters nothing on line 42 and $0 is their honest answer). It exists so the upfront refusal can distinguish "no carry-in" from "carry-in not yet asked".

Fact.Name: Whether this filer has supplied a Form 5329 line 42 carry-in ABOVE zero
Fact.Description: Answered AND positive. It is deliberately stricter than ../hsaPriorYearExcessCarryInAnswered, which is answeredness alone, and the difference is the point of this fact: a legitimate $0 from one spouse is an ANSWER, so an answeredness-only test would let one spouse's $0 satisfy the refusal while the spouse who actually holds the carry-in was never asked.

Fact.Name: Whether some filer has supplied a Form 5329 line 42 carry-in above zero
Fact.Description:
The upfront yes/no /hasHsaExcessContributionsPreviousYear is a RETURN-level question, so it cannot say WHICH spouse holds the carry-in; this is the matching return-level test over the two per-filer amounts.
IT TESTS FOR A POSITIVE AMOUNT, NOT MERE ANSWEREDNESS. An Any over the two per-filer IsCompletes would be defeated by a joint return: the return answers YES, the primary legitimately answers $0, the secondary - who holds the carry-in - is never asked, and the Any goes true, the guard goes false, both line 42s stay $0 and the 6% tax vanishes silently. A return-level YES asserts that SOMEBODY has a carry-in, so "somebody supplied a positive amount" is the matching test, and every state short of it is refused.
BOTH READS ARE FENCED. A BARE operand, on a return that has fewer filer items than the read names - a ONE-filer return for the secondary read, a NO-filer return for both - is Incomplete, so Any(false, Incomplete) would be Incomplete. That is not a completeness curiosity here, because this fact is negated inside /hsaPriorYearExcessCarryInUnsupplied, which gates BOTH /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions and the line 49 suppression: an Incomplete here would turn a REFUSAL into a fall-through, and a return that answered the upfront carry-in question YES and supplied no amount would file a Placeholder line 49 instead of being blocked. The primary read sits inside All(IsComplete(p), p) and the secondary inside All(isFilingStatusMFJ, IsComplete(s), s) - the Boolean idiom the 8z leg uses, and the MFJ conjunct the return-level Add idiom uses, because on an MFS return each spouse files their own 1040 and only a joint return has a second filer whose carry-in belongs on this return.

Fact.Name: The return says a prior-year carry-in exists and no filer has supplied its amount
Fact.Description:
Slice (1) of /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions, lifted into its own return-level fact so that TWO consumers can read it: the guard, which blocks submission, and /filers/*/hsaForm5329Line49ExciseTax, which must contribute $0 to Schedule 2 line 8 for a return the guard is refusing. Without the second consumer an upfront YES with no amount supplied would put a line-47 excise tax on a refused return's printed total.
IT READS ONLY the upfront yes/no and the amount-supplied test above, so it cannot reach /filers/*/mayHaveHsaContributions and cannot close the resolution cycle that /filers/*/hsaAnsweredTaxYearContributionSignal exists to avoid.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE: the IsComplete conjunct leads.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 42 - prior-year excess contributions carried into 2025
Fact.Description: This filer's Form 5329 line 42. Complete-safe $0 when the carry-in has not been supplied; the return that answers "yes" upfront and supplies nothing is refused by /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions rather than filed on this $0.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 43 - unused 2025 contribution room that absorbs the carry-in
Fact.Description:
This filer's Form 5329 line 43: the amount by which their Form 8889 line 12 contribution limit exceeds their Form 8889 line 2 contributions, floored at zero. Room left under the current year's limit absorbs a prior-year excess, which is why line 45 subtracts it from line 42.
THE INSTRUCTION'S SECOND HALF directs "include on your 2025 Form 8889, line 13, the smaller of: Form 5329, line 43; or the excess, if any, of Form 5329, line 42, over Form 5329, line 44" - i.e. the absorbed carry-in becomes DEDUCTIBLE this year. ../hsaTotalDeductibleAmount adds LesserOf(this line, the excess of line 42 over line 44) as a second term, so the absorbed dollars are deductible in the year they are absorbed and the excise base is unchanged.
WHY LINE 12 AND NOT LINE 3: the instruction names line 12 in as many words ("Your contribution limit for HSAs is the amount on line 12 of Form 8889"), and line 12 is line 8 already reduced by the employer contributions and funding distributions of line 11. Reading line 3 here would ignore that reduction and absorb more carry-in than the form allows.
A DEPENDENT FILER'S LINE 43 IS $0, the LEADING ARM OF THE SWITCH BELOW. It uses NEITHER line 12 nor line 2, so it does not contradict the paragraph above - it precedes it. A claimable dependent who has made HSA contributions can file (see ../hasHsaContributionsAndCanBeClaimedAsDependent), so this line must state their absorption. WHY $0, and the argument is a difference between two statutory phrases rather than a claim that one phrase must mean the same thing twice. IRC 106(d)(1) caps the employer exclusion at "the limitation under section 223(b) (determined without regard to this subsection)" - a LIMITATION, an amount stated by 223(b)(1) to (b)(5), which 223(b)(6) does not touch. IRC 4973(g)(2)(B)(i) keys THIS line to something else: "the maximum amount allowable as a deduction under section 223(b) (determined without regard to section 106(d))". 223(b)(6) says "No deduction shall be allowed under this section" to a dependent, so the second quantity is $0 for them while the first is untouched - which is why, on the statutory reading, (b)(6) leaves the employer exclusion alone while the carry-in absorbs nothing. THE PRINTED CHAIN REACHES $0 TOO, by its own route: the instruction keys line 43 to Form 8889 line 12, and for a dependent the printed line 12 is $0 because the Line 3 Limitation Chart routes dependency through ELIGIBILITY to a $0 line 3. So this arm is $0 under BOTH coherent readings and nothing here turns on which of them governs (interpretation: owner ruling, see TAX-INTERPRETATIONS-FOR-EXPERT-REVIEW.md AD-02, which follows the printed chain); the tag on the authority block is interpretation:provisional because the arm's TRIGGER, ../hsaDeductionDeniedAsDependent, embodies the statutory reading.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0 when either input is Incomplete, which is the state of every filer who has not reached the contributions section.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 44 - 2025 taxable HSA distributions (Form 8889 line 16)
Fact.Description:
This filer's Form 5329 line 44, which the form defines by pointer: "2025 distributions from your HSAs from Form 8889, line 16". Line 16 already ships as ../taxableHsaDistributionTotal. A distribution of a prior-year excess taken this year is taxable on line 16 and reduces the carry-in through line 45, which is why the two lines are added there rather than either being ignored.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0: line 16 is deliberately left undefined for a filer with no distributions at all (see ../taxableHsaDistributionTotal), so it is read behind an IsComplete.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 45 - what the carry-in is measured against
Fact.Description: This filer's Form 5329 line 45, "Add lines 43 and 44": the unused 2025 contribution room plus the 2025 taxable distributions, which together are what reduces the prior-year excess on line 46.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 46 - the prior-year excess still in the account
Fact.Description: This filer's Form 5329 line 46, "Prior year excess contributions. Subtract line 45 from line 42. If zero or less, enter -0-". The floor at zero is printed, so a carry-in more than absorbed by 2025 room and distributions leaves nothing to tax.

Fact.Name: IRC 4973(g)(1) - a dependent filer's OWN contributions, excess in full
Fact.Description:
This filer's Form 8889 line 2 in FULL, when IRC 223(b)(6) denies them the section 223 deduction; $0 for everybody else.
WHY THE WHOLE OF LINE 2 AND NOT THE PART OVER A LIMIT. IRC 4973(g)(1) defines an HSA excess contribution as the amount contributed "which is neither excludable from gross income under section 106(d) nor allowable as a deduction under section 223 for such year". A dependent's OWN contribution is neither: it is not employer-paid, so 106(d) never reaches it, and 223(b)(6) denies the section 223 deduction outright. So every dollar of it is excess, whatever the 223(b) limitation is. This fact covers the OWN contribution only; the EMPLOYER's contribution keeps its own path (the over-limit gross, and ../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled for the income leg).
THE PRINTED LINE 47 ARITHMETIC REACHES THE SAME ANSWER BY A DIFFERENT ROUTE. The Form 5329 Line 47 instruction computes the excess as line 2 "over your contribution limit (Form 8889, line 12)", and the Form 8889 Line 3 Limitation Chart routes a dependent through ELIGIBILITY to a $0 line 3, hence a $0 line 12, hence all of line 2 as excess. So the OWN-contribution answer is the same under the statutory reading (223(b)(6) as a deduction denial) and under the printed chain, and nothing here turns on which of them governs. The EMPLOYER leg is where they differ, and it is decided for the printed chain - interpretation: owner ruling, see TAX-INTERPRETATIONS-FOR-EXPERT-REVIEW.md AD-02: a dependent's employer code W contribution is line 47 excess, with line 3 $0, and a claimable dependent's line 12 is $0 on both routes.
WHAT THIS FACT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT REACH, so the omission is not read as an oversight: the EMPLOYER leg of Form 8889 line 11 - a box 12 code W contribution and a qualified HSA funding distribution alike. Line 47 takes the GREATER of this fact and the over-limit gross, so a dependent whose line 11 exceeds their line 8 limit is measured the over-limit way, reaches Schedule 1 line 8z for that excess (/hsaSchedule1Line8zEmployerExcessOtherIncome) as well as the Form 5329 Part VII excise, and is refused only in the narrower ../causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled slice.
THE GATE IS /hsaCoverageAndContributionsSectionIsComplete, the same conjunct the sibling over-limit cause ../hsaContributionsOverLimitAndComplete carries, and for the same measured reason: this dictionary does not treat a filer's Form 8889 Part I as settled until the coverage-and-contributions section is answered, and the six committed hsa-testing-period fixtures are the record of what charging tax against an unsettled Part I costs. ../hsaDependentOwnContributionsAnswered is the second conjunct, so an unanswered line 2 yields $0 here - which is safe only because those two guards REFUSE that return.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0: every conjunct is complete-safe false and the default arm is $0.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 47 - excess contributions for 2025
Fact.Description:
This filer's Form 5329 line 47: their 2025 contributions over their 2025 contribution limit, LESS the part withdrawn in time, floored at zero.
THE ARITHMETIC AND WHY IT IS ONE SUBTRACTION AND NOT TWO. The instruction reads the excess as Form 8889 line 2 over Form 8889 line 12 and then says "Also include on line 47 any excess contributions your employer made". Line 12 is line 8 less line 11, so (line 2 - line 12) + (line 11 - line 8) is (line 2 + line 11) - line 8, which is exactly the shipping ../hsaContributionLimitExceededAmount: total contributions less the Form 8889 line 8 limit. The identity holds through line 12's own floor at zero, because whatever line 12's floor removes is precisely the employer excess the second sentence adds back.
"UNLESS WITHDRAWN" IS THE BOUNDARY WITH /hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome. An excess withdrawn by the due date with its earnings "will be treated as not having been contributed", so it is subtracted here; the EARNINGS on it are income under IRC 223(f)(3)(A) and are carried by that other fact, not by this one. The two halves of Pub 969's paired rule therefore land on different lines of different forms and neither double-counts the other. THE AMOUNT SUBTRACTED IS NET OF THE EARNINGS. Form 8889 line 14b - and the shipping ../hsaTotalExcessContributionsWithdrawnInTime built on it - carries "any excess contributions (AND THE EARNINGS on those excess contributions) ... withdrawn by the due date", and the per-item writable's own Description says the same ("Amount of excess contributions and earnings on them withdrawn"). Only the CONTRIBUTIONS are "treated as not having been contributed"; the earnings are income under IRC 223(f)(3)(A) and are carried by /hsaExcessContributionEarningsOtherIncome. Subtracting the gross figure would remove the earnings from the excise base too and understate the tax by 6% of them on every partial return. What is subtracted here is therefore ../hsaExcessContributionsWithdrawnInTimeNetOfEarnings. Line 14b's OTHER half, an IRC 223(f)(5) rollover, is not a return of an excess and is in neither figure.
THE GATE IS ../hsaContributionsOverLimitAndComplete, NOT A BARE IsComplete PAIR, and the difference is MEASURED. That shipping fact is All(/hsaCoverageAndContributionsSectionIsComplete, ../hsaContributionLimitExceeded), and the section-completeness half is load-bearing: this dictionary does not treat a filer's Form 8889 line 8 limitation as settled until the coverage-and-contributions section is answered, and an excess measured against a half-answered limit is a number the filer never finished supplying inputs for. A gate of All(IsComplete(limit), IsComplete(contributions)) instead charges $180 on the six committed hsa-testing-period fixtures, whose filers report a $3,000 qualified HSA funding distribution against an unsettled limit and are refused upstream by /flowKnockoutHdhpCoverageNotAllYear.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0: ../hsaContributionsOverLimitAndComplete is a Switch whose default is False, so an unanswered return takes the zero arm.
THE SECOND GROSS is ../hsaDependentOwnContributionExcess, a dependent filer's Form 8889 line 2 in full, which IRC 4973(g)(1) makes excess whatever the limit is because 223(b)(6) denies the deduction. GREATER-OF AND NOT ADD, and the arithmetic is why rather than taste. Statutory excess for a dependent is own + max($0, employer - line 8 limit): the own contributions are never deductible, and the employer's are excludable under 106(d) only up to the 223(b) limitation. GreaterOf(max($0, total - limit), own) equals that identically in both branches - where employer >= limit both are own + employer - limit, and where employer < limit both are own - while Add would double-count the own contribution on every over-limit dependent.
THE WITHDRAWN SUBTRACTION IS ONE SUBTRACTION and sits outside both grosses, on the larger of them, with the floor at $0 printed once. A timely-returned excess is "treated as not having been contributed" whichever gross produced it, so subtracting inside one arm and not the other would make the relief depend on which limb happened to win.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 48 - total excess contributions
Fact.Description: This filer's Form 5329 line 48, "Total excess contributions. Add lines 46 and 47" - the prior-year carry-in that survived line 45 plus this year's own excess. It is also the figure that becomes NEXT year's line 42, which is why the form asks for it as a total rather than taxing the two halves separately.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 49 - the smaller of line 48 and the December 31 account value
Fact.Description:
The multiplicand of line 49: "the smaller of line 48 or the value of your HSAs on December 31, 2025 (including 2025 contributions made in 2026)".
THE CAP BINDS ONLY WHEN THE DECEMBER 31 VALUE IS ANSWERED, and this filer's own ../causesHsaForm5329Line49AccountValueUnsupplied refuses the return before this fact's terminal Case (line 48 unbounded) can be reached on a filed return: see that fact and ../writableHsaDecember31AccountValue for why the value is required rather than optional once line 48 is positive.

Fact.Name: This filer has a positive Form 5329 line 48 excess and no December 31 account value to cap it
Fact.Description:
A pure detector, read only by ../hsaForm5329Line49ExciseTax (downstream) and by /flowKnockoutHsaForm5329Line49AccountValueUnsupplied (a STANDALONE knockout, not by /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions itself - reading this fact's own inputs from THAT guard closes a resolution cycle; see the standalone knockout's Description for the measured failure). IRC 4973(a)'s flush text and Form 5329 line 49 both make the December 31 account value a MANDATORY input once there is an excess to tax, not an optional relief - "shall not exceed 6 percent of the value of the account ... determined as of the close of the taxable year" is not phrased as an election. True only when this filer's line 48 is positive AND ../writableHsaDecember31AccountValue has not been answered.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE: ../hsaForm5329Line48TotalExcess carries a True default arm and cannot be Incomplete, so GreaterThan(it, $0) cannot be Incomplete either.

Fact.Name: A filer's Form 5329 line 48 excess with no December 31 account value to cap it - standalone
Fact.Description: Blocks submission when either filer's Form 5329 line 48 shows an HSA excess contribution but the December 31 value of that filer's HSAs (line 49's cap) was not supplied. The filer supplies the account value and the excise tax computes. The primary filer's detector is read through a count of the /filers items that are the primary filer and trip it, which is Complete on every return; the secondary filer's detector is read only on a joint return, because only a joint return carries the spouse's Form 5329, and is a Complete false otherwise.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 line 49 - this filer's own 6% excise tax
Fact.Description:
This filer's Form 5329 line 49, 6% of ../hsaForm5329Line49CapAmount, rounded on THEIR OWN FORM.
WHY THE ROUNDING IS PER FILER RATHER THAN ONCE ON THE COUPLE'S TOTAL. Form 5329 is filed by an individual - its own name line reads "Name of individual subject to additional tax" - so on a joint return where both spouses owe this tax there are TWO Forms 5329, each printing its own line 49, and Schedule 2 line 8 carries their total. The 1040 instructions' rounding rule is stated of amounts entered on "your return and schedules" and requires that if you round at all you "must round all amounts", which is what makes each printed line 49 a whole dollar before the two are added. The numbers differ: two spouses each with a line 48 of $175.00 print $11 and $11 for a total of $22, where 6% of the summed $350.00 is $21.00. The fixture hsa-5329-partvii-mfj-per-spouse-rounding-differs is exactly that case. This is the same placement, for the same reason, that /filers/*/hsaTestingPeriodFailureAdditionalTax uses for Form 8889 line 21.
$0 FOR A FILER WHOSE RETURN IS REFUSED, and that is the one rule that keeps the printed total honest. The arm reads four residual refusals: ../causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled (the employer-excess detector AND a Form 8889 line 10 funding distribution above the line 8 limitation whose cap cannot be computed - a plain employer excess files with its income add-back at /hsaSchedule1Line8zEmployerExcessOtherIncome and therefore carries its 6% excise); ../causesHsaPriorYearExcessAbsorptionUncomputable (a carry-in whose 2025 limit cannot be measured); /hsaPriorYearExcessCarryInUnsupplied (a return-level YES whose carry-in AMOUNT nobody supplied - without it an over-limit filer on such a return would move Schedule 2 line 8 while the guard was refusing); and ../causesHsaForm5329Line49AccountValueUnsupplied (a positive line 48 with no December 31 account value supplied, gating the STANDALONE /flowKnockoutHsaForm5329Line49AccountValueUnsupplied, not /flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions itself - see that fact's own Description for the cycle this avoids). All four mean the return does not file, and a partial tax on a return that does not file would move Schedule 2 line 8 for a population this dictionary has not finished computing. Lines 42 to 48 keep their true values either way, so the arithmetic is still witnessed by the fixtures; only the printed line 49 is suppressed. MEASURED: without this arm the six committed hsa-testing-period fixtures - whose filers hold a $3,000 qualified HSA funding distribution against a $0 line 8 limitation and are refused - each gain $180 on taxCalculations:/line21OfSchedule2.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION: every input is complete-safe $0 or complete-safe false.

Fact.Name: Form 5329 Part VII - the 6% excise tax on excess HSA contributions (Schedule 2 line 8)
Fact.Description:
Both filers' Form 5329 line 49, summed for Schedule 2 (Form 1040) line 8, which reaches Schedule 2 line 21 and then Form 1040 line 23. THE DESTINATION IS THE ONE THE FORM PRINTS and the one this dictionary already reaches for Form 5329: line 49 says "Include this amount on Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 8", and form5329:/form5329AdditionalTaxOnEarlyDistributions (Form 5329 Part I line 4) is already an addend of taxCalculations:/line21OfSchedule2 on that same printed line. It is NOT Schedule 2 line 17c (the 20% tax on unqualified distributions, /hsaCollectionRouteAdditionalTax20PctTotal) and NOT line 17d (the 10% testing-period tax, /hsaTestingPeriodFailureAdditionalTax); routing to either would double-book a live line.
THE ROUNDING HAPPENS PER FILER AND THIS FACT ONLY ADDS, for the reason set out on /filers/*/hsaForm5329Line49ExciseTax: Form 5329 is an individual's form.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0 on every return that answers nothing.

Fact.Name: Whether this filer's own intake says they put anything into an HSA for 2025
Fact.Description:
The "did you contribute for 2025" question read at its SOURCE: this filer's box-12 code-W total from their W-2s, or their own answer to the non-W-2 contributions question. It is deliberately NOT ../hasMadeContributionsToHsa, which means the same thing but reaches it through ../mayHaveHsaContributions and therefore through Not(/flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions): reading that fact from anything the guard depends on closes a resolution cycle. This fact exists only so ../causesHsaPriorYearExcessAbsorptionUncomputable can ask the question without closing it.
FAIL-CLOSED: an unanswered non-W-2 question reads false, not Incomplete, so the caller refuses rather than proceeding on an unknown.

Fact.Name: Whether this filer's 2025 HSA contributions question has an answer
Fact.Description: Whether this filer's "did you contribute for 2025" question is settled at its source: box-12 code-W contributions on their W-2s, or ANY answer (yes or no) to the non-W-2 contributions question. It is the answered-ness of ../hsaAnsweredTaxYearContributionSignal and reads the same raw intakes, so it stays outside the flow loop that ../hasMadeContributionsToHsa closes. An unanswered question reads false (fail-closed).

Fact.Name: A carry-in this return cannot measure against a 2025 limit
Fact.Description:
True for a filer who supplied a Form 5329 line 42 carry-in ABOVE zero and has not answered the 2025 HSA contributions question at all (../hsaTaxYearContributionQuestionAnswered false). Form 5329 line 43 absorbs a carry-in with the room left under the filer's Form 8889 line 12 limit. Form 8889 Part I is owed to a filer with a carry-in whether or not they contributed (../hsaForm8889PartIRequired), so a filer who answered that they made no 2025 contributions has line 12, line 43 and the line 13 absorbed deduction computed. Where the contributions question has no answer, the room cannot be measured until line 2 is known, and line 43 would silently be $0, which absorbs nothing and taxes the whole carry-in: the taxpayer-ADVERSE direction. So the return is refused instead, and the refusal is a missing-input one that the answer retires.
WHY IT DOES NOT READ ../hasMadeContributionsToHsa. That fact conjoins ../mayHaveHsaContributions, which conjoins Not(/flowKnockoutHsaExcessContributions) - the very guard this fact feeds - so reading it closes a resolution cycle (measured: a version of this fact that read it sent every form8889 case to "Maximum call stack size exceeded"). The contributions question is read off the raw intake instead, which is outside the flow loop by construction.

Fact.Name: An employer contribution over the Form 8889 line 8 limit - the income add-back's population
Fact.Description:
True for a filer who is over their contribution limit AND whose employer contributions and qualified HSA funding distributions (Form 8889 line 11) alone exceed their Form 8889 line 8 limitation. That is the "excess employer contributions" case: where the excess "was not included in income on Form W-2, you must report it as 'Other income' on your tax return". The add-back ships at /hsaSchedule1Line8zEmployerExcessOtherIncome, priced per filer at ../hsaEmployerExcessContributionAmount and wired to Schedule 1 line 9 through income:/schedule1TotalOtherIncome.
THIS FACT REFUSES NOTHING. It is the POPULATION DETECTOR for the income leg - the exact role /filers/*/archerMsaEmployerExcessContributionsExist plays for the Archer twin. Its path name is historical and is kept, because a rename is a delete plus an add, which would owe the refusal allowlists and the completeness-probe baseline for no behaviour change. What /flowHsaContributionsOverLimitKnockout aggregates, and what suppresses ../hsaForm5329Line49ExciseTax, is the narrower ../causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled: this fact AND a line 10 qualified HSA funding distribution above the line 8 limitation whose exclusion cap cannot be computed.
THE TEST IS A CONJUNCT ON THE OVER-LIMIT CAUSE, not a replacement for it: ../hsaContributionsOverLimitAndComplete feeds the two summary-table visibility facts, so the interview shows the overage to every over-limit filer.

Fact.Name: The AMOUNT of this filer's excess employer HSA contributions
Fact.Description:
The excess employer HSA contribution this filer owes as Other income: "the excess, if any, of your employer's contributions over your limitation on line 8", where "if you made a qualified HSA funding distribution (line 10) during the tax year, reduce your limitation (line 8) by that distribution/contribution before you determine whether you have excess employer contributions". Its population is ../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled.
THE ARITHMETIC IS line 11 LESS GreaterOf(line 8, line 10) - the i8889 sentence read to its end. Form 8889 line 11 is line 9 (the employer's contributions) plus line 10 (the qualified HSA funding distribution), so for a filer whose line 10 is at or under line 8, line 11 - line 8 = line 9 - (line 8 - line 10), which is the instruction's own sentence: the employer's contributions over the limitation reduced by the funding distribution; no separate line 9 read is needed. A reduced limitation cannot go below zero, so where line 10 exceeds line 8 the reduced limitation is $0 and the excess EMPLOYER contribution is line 11 - line 10 = line 9, the employer's own contributions and nothing else. The funding distribution's overflow is not an employer contribution at all: it is income on Form 1040 line 4b (see ../causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled). Reading line 8 bare would report that overflow TWICE, once on Form 1040 line 4b as the un-excluded part of the IRA distribution and again on Schedule 1 line 8z as employer compensation.
IT IS THE SAME SUBTRACTION THE DETECTING BOOLEAN DOES, expressed once with a floor. That boolean keeps its own body rather than being rewritten as GreaterThan(this, 0).
IT FEEDS ONE PLACE AND DOES NOT DOUBLE-COUNT THE 6% EXCISE. This amount is INCOME because an employer contribution over the section 223(b) limitation was never excludable under IRC 106(d)(1) in the first place; the same dollars are also inside the Form 5329 line 47/48 excise base, which is a different tax on one amount. i8889 and Pub 969 impose both in the same paragraph, and the Archer twin makes the identical pairing. THE SAME PAIRING REACHES A FUNDING DISTRIBUTION, with its own authority: where a qualified HSA funding distribution exceeds the IRC 408(d)(9)(C)(i) cap, the over-cap part is income on Form 1040 line 4b AND is inside the Form 5329 line 47/48 excise base at the same time. That is not a double count: IRC 4973(g)(1) defines an HSA excess contribution as the amount contributed "which is neither excludable from gross income under section 106(d) nor allowable as a deduction under section 223 for such year", and the over-cap part of a funding distribution is neither - 408(d)(9)(C)(i) is exactly what stops it being excludable, and 223 gives no deduction for a transfer the filer did not contribute out of income. So one amount carries the 4973(a)(5) 6% excise and the 408(d)(9) income inclusion, on the same footing as the employer excess.
COMPLETE-SAFE ON A RETURN WITH NO HSA: ../hsaEmployerContributionsAndFundingDistributionTotal is "always complete" by its own Description and is $0 there; ../hsaTotalContributionLimit can be Incomplete, which is what ../hsaEmployerExcessContributionAmountOrZero fences.

Fact.Name: The excess employer HSA contribution for the Schedule 1 sum, 0 when it does not resolve
Fact.Description:
../hsaEmployerExcessContributionAmount fenced with IsComplete, so the return-level Other-income sum stays complete-safe on every return whose Form 8889 line 8 limitation is not settled.
PROVABLY LOSSLESS FOR THIS FACT'S ONE CONSUMER. The 8z leg reads this only inside an arm gated on ../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled, and that fact's own Switch requires IsComplete on BOTH line 8 and line 11 before it can be true - so the fence can only fire for a filer the gate has already excluded, whose contribution to the sum is $0 either way.

Fact.Name: Writable: the excess employer HSA contribution is already included in W-2 box 1 wages
Fact.Description:
The condition i8889 and Pub 969 both put on the Other-income report: "If the excess was not included in income on Form W-2, you must report it as 'Other income' on your tax return"; Pub 969 spells the box out - "If the excess contribution isn't included in Form W-2, box 1 you must report the excess as 'Other income' on your tax return."
NO FORM LINE SUPPLIES IT. The amount reaches this dictionary through W-2 box 12 code W, which is by construction the figure the employer treated as EXCLUDED from box 1, and nothing on the W-2 says whether the employer noticed the excess and taxed it anyway. So this is a question the application must ask, not a field to read.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE WHEN UNANSWERED, i.e. the default assumption is that the excess was not already taxed and must be reported. That is the taxpayer-ADVERSE direction, and it is also the ordinary case for the reason just given. A filer whose employer did include it says so and the leg drops to $0; the 6% excise on the same dollars is unaffected either way, because IRC 4973(g)(1) makes an amount excess when it is "neither excludable from gross income under section 106(d) nor allowable as a deduction under section 223", and an amount the employer put in box 1 was not excludable.
WHY ONE RETURN-LEVEL ANSWER RATHER THAN ONE PER FILER: the leg it gates is a single Schedule 1 line 8z amount, the question is about how one employer filled in one W-2, and splitting it per filer would ask a joint couple two versions of a question whose only effect is on their combined line 9. NAMED GAP, the same one the Archer twin names as G14: a joint return where one spouse's employer included the excess and the other's did not cannot express that, and answering yes there would drop BOTH legs. The adverse answer (leave it false) is always available and is the default.

Fact.Name: The return says the excess employer HSA contribution is already in W-2 wages
Fact.Description: /writableHsaEmployerExcessAlreadyInW2Income made complete-safe FALSE, so an unanswered return reports the excess as Other income rather than dropping it. The adverse default is argued on the writable.

Fact.Name: Schedule 1 LINE 8z — the excess employer HSA contribution as "Other income"
Fact.Description:
Both filers' excess employer HSA contributions, reported as Other income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040) line 8z unless the return says the employer already included the amount in W-2 box 1 wages.
LINE 8z, NOT 8f. Line 8f is the Form 8889 line, and the two Form 8889 amounts this dictionary already routes there - line 16 taxable distributions and line 20 testing-period income - are printed lines of the form. This amount is not on Form 8889 at all: the instructions name no line for it, they say only "report it as 'Other income' on your tax return", and Schedule 1 line 8z is this dictionary's - and the Form 1040 instructions' - residual Other-income line. NAMED as an interpretation rather than a citation: no IRS text says "8z" for this amount. The Archer twin reaches the same place from the identical i8853 sentence.
THE 223(f)(3) TIMELY WITHDRAWAL DOES NOT REDUCE THIS LEG, and that is a determination rather than an omission. i8889's relief bullets let a filer withdraw the excess employer contribution and have it "treated as if they had not been contributed" only if, among other conditions, "you do not claim an exclusion from income for the amount of the withdrawn contributions" - that is, the amount stays in income. Pub 969 states the scope of the relief directly: the filer may withdraw "and avoid paying the EXCISE TAX on the amount withdrawn". IRC 223(f)(3) agrees: what it disapplies is paragraph (2)'s INCLUSION OF THE DISTRIBUTION in gross income, and the net income accompanying it is expressly included in gross income anyway. So the withdrawal moves the Form 5329 line 47/48 excise base - which the shipping /filers/*/hsaExcessContributionsWithdrawnInTimeNetOfEarnings already does - and leaves this line alone. Fixture hsa-employer-excess-withdrawn-in-time-keeps-the-other-income pins both halves at once.
THE SINGLE Round IS HERE, following the i1040gi rule the Schedule 1 line 23 sibling cites: include cents when adding and round the total once. The per-filer amounts keep their cents.
COMPLETE-SAFE $0 ON EVERY RETURN OUTSIDE THE POPULATION, gated FIRST rather than arithmetically: the leading arm reads only the two filers' ../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled, each a Switch whose default is False, so a return with no HSA takes the $0 arm without touching a placeholder-backed HSA input - the same ordering the Archer twin uses.
$0 ON A RETURN THAT DOES NOT FILE, and that arm is MEASURED rather than reasoned. The second arm drops this leg to $0 whenever either filer trips /filers/*/causesHsaFundingDistributionExcessIncomeUnmodeled - the residual /flowHsaContributionsOverLimitKnockout refuses - for exactly the reason /filers/*/hsaForm5329Line49ExciseTax suppresses its own printed line: moving Schedule 1 line 9 for a population this dictionary has not finished computing is worse than moving nothing. Without it the five committed hsa-testing-period fixtures, whose filers hold a $3,000 qualified HSA funding distribution against a $0 line 8 limitation and are refused, each gain $3,000 on income:/schedule1TotalOtherIncome.
MFJ, NOT MARRIED. The secondary filer's amount joins only on a joint return. On an MFS return the spouse's excess employer contribution is income on the SPOUSE's own return, which this dictionary does not model; summing /filers/* would put it on this filer's line 9. Same idiom, same reason, as /hsaExcessContributionExciseTaxForm5329PartVii. SINGLE-FILER RETURNS: both secondary reads sit inside All(filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ, IsComplete(x), x), the idiom /hsaExcessContributionExciseTaxForm5329PartVii ships. THE PRIMARY READ IS FENCED TOO: a scenario with no /filers item at all (the L2 strategies spike) has no /primaryFiler item either, so the primary cause is Incomplete and Any(Incomplete, false) would be Incomplete. Both primary reads sit inside All(IsComplete(p), p), which is Complete false when p is Incomplete. Where p resolves at all (every return with a filer), the fence is transparent.

Fact.Name: A line 10 funding distribution above the line 8 limit, whose overflow is not employer income
Fact.Description:
THE RESIDUAL /flowHsaContributionsOverLimitKnockout KEEPS: a line 10 funding distribution above the line 8 limitation whose IRC 408(d)(9)(C)(i) exclusion cap cannot be computed. It is a printed-LINE question rather than a missing amount.
WHERE THE BOUNDARY IS. ../hsaEmployerExcessContributionAmount's arithmetic, line 11 less line 8, is re-expressed by the i8889 instruction as the employer's line 9 contributions over the limitation reduced by the line 10 qualified HSA funding distribution. That re-expression holds only while line 10 is at or under line 8. Once the funding distribution ALONE exceeds the limitation, the difference stops being an employer contribution - it overflows line 9 - and the overflow is an IRA distribution, not compensation.
WHY THAT OVERFLOW CANNOT GO TO SCHEDULE 1 LINE 8z. IRC 408(d)(9)(A) excludes a qualified HSA funding distribution from gross income, and 408(d)(9)(C)(i) caps that exclusion: "the amount excluded from gross income by subparagraph (A) shall not exceed" the section 223(b) annual limitation computed on the coverage in force AT THE TIME OF THE TRANSFER. The uncapped part is therefore includible - but as an IRA distribution on Form 1040 line 4b, which is where this dictionary already routes an unexcluded funding distribution (form1099Rs:/form1099Rs/*/line4cHfdExclusion), and not as employer compensation on Schedule 1 line 8z. Putting it on 8z would file the amount on the wrong printed line; leaving it off entirely would understate the return.
Every filer this fact is true for also trips ../causesHsaEmployerExcessContributionsIncomeUnmodeled, its first conjunct.
COMPLETE-SAFE FALSE: the Switch default is False, and the guarded arm reads line 8 only after that conjunct - itself a Switch requiring IsComplete on line 8 - is true.
WHAT THIS FACT REFUSES IS EXACTLY THE OTHER TWO CONJUNCTS OF ../hsaFundingDistributionExclusionCapComputable, and each is an ANSWER this return does not hold rather than a computation this repo cannot do: (1) NO MONTHLY COVERAGE VECTOR (/hsaLine3VectorGoverns false). The (C)(i) basis is a per-month coverage type and the vector is the only place this dictionary carries one. That fact is an ANSWEREDNESS gate over /filers/*/hsaMonthlyCoverageVectorAnswered, so the population shrinks when the screen ships and never on a dictionary edit. (2) THE TRANSFER MONTH UNANSWERED (../hsaFundingDistributionTransferMonthAnswered false) - asked-and-not-answered, the correct-refusal residue. A TRANSFER MONTH IN WHICH THE FILER HELD NO COVERAGE (../hsaFundingDistributionTransferMonthChartAmount not above $0, a filer who was not an eligible individual, or was on Medicare, at the time of the transfer) DOES NOT REFUSE. ../hsaFundingDistributionExclusionCapComputable treats that population as computable, and ../hsaFundingDistributionExclusionCap computes a genuine $0 for it (the substituted chart's own arithmetic, argued in full at ../hsaFundingDistributionExclusionCapComputable), so ../line4cHfdExclusion clamps to $0 and the whole Form 8889 line 10 amount is includible on Form 1040 line 4b without this fact's refusal.
THE MARRIED RULES' SPOUSE-ELIGIBILITY CONDITION. Pub. 969 (2025) carries the caution that "The rules for married people apply only if both spouses are eligible individuals" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p969.pdf, page 6, RIGHT column); on this (C)(i) chain it is tested by ../spouseIsHsaEligibleIndividual, a conjunct of ../hsaHfdCapMarriedRefinementsApply.

Fact.Name: The month of a qualified HSA funding distribution
Fact.Description: The twelve months of the tax year, which is the whole of what IRC 408(d)(9)(C)(i) needs from the filer: the month whose HDHP coverage type the cap is computed on. There is NO `none` option and no "did not make one" option, deliberately - the question is only ever asked of a filer whose Form 8889 line 10 is above $0, and a filer who made no transfer answers the line 10 question instead. An unanswered month is therefore a missing answer and is REFUSED rather than defaulted; see ../hsaFundingDistributionExclusionCapComputable.

Fact.Name: The month in which this filer's qualified HSA funding distribution was transferred
Fact.Description:
User response, and the ONE discriminating intake IRC 408(d)(9)(C)(i) needs: "In which month of 2025 did the trustee transfer the money from your IRA into your HSA?"
WHY THE MONTH AND NOTHING MORE. The twelve-month coverage vector (../hsaCoverageTypeMonth01 through 12)
already carries the HDHP coverage type the filer held on the first day of every month, which is the fact the cap is "computed on the basis of". What the return does not carry is WHICH of those twelve months the transfer happened in, and no form line supplies it - the Form 1099-R has no distribution date in this dictionary and Form 8889 line 10 is a year total. That is exactly an application question, and it is the only one the cap needs.
